utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, everyone. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. This is the beginning of the week. My greetings to all the people in the courtroom, the OTP, the Defence counsel, and the accused, as well as all the people in and outside this courtroom helping us. First of all, I'm going to give the floor to the registrar. He has a few IC numbers for us.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours. Several parties have submitted lists of documents to be tendered through Witness BC. The list submitted by OTP shall be given Exhibit number 565 under seal. The list submitted by 1D shall be given Exhibit number IC 566 under seal. The list submitted by 2D shall be given Exhibit number IC 567 under seal. The list submitted by 3D shall be given Exhibit number IC 568 under seal. The list submitted by 4D shall be given Exhibit number IC 569 under seal. The list submitted by 5D shall be given Exhibit number IC 570 under seal. And, finally, the list submitted by 6D shall be given Exhibit number IC 571 under seal. In addition, some parties have submitted lists of documents to be tendered through Witness Salim Delalic. The list submitted by OTP shall be given Exhibit number IC 572, while the list submitted by 3D shall be given Exhibit number 573. Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Registrar. One reminder with relation to a procedural matter. On the 2nd of May we received from the Defence a motion or request for certification on appeal regarding Witness BB. Today, the Defence filed a supplemental document with submissions within the same framework. Initially the Prosecution had been given until the date of the 23rd of May to reply. Now that we have supplemental submissions, we extend, if need be, this delay to the 30th of May. Thereby the Prosecution will have until the 30th of May to file its reply. Regarding the coming witness - he's going to come into the courtroom in a few moments - the Prosecution will have five hours as requested in its filings. As to the Defence, they will have all together seven hours to be divided as follows: For Prlic, two hours; for the Petkovic Defence, one hour and a half; for the Praljak Defence, one hour -- one hour and 30 minutes; 40 minutes for the other accused. So all together you have seven hours. Of course, the accused through their counsel may decide to spread the time differently. It's for them to decide according to their needs. At any rate, I remind that Prlic has two hours; Petkovic, one hour and 30 minutes; same amount for Mr. Praljak; Mr. Stojic, 40 minutes; Mr. Coric, 40 minutes; and, Mr. Pusic, 40 minutes. So much for this witness who is scheduled for the whole week. I am pleased to see Mr. Scott again. He wasn't there last time. I would like to say to Mr. Mundis that following the ruling of the Appeals Chamber confirming the time given to the Prosecution by the Trial Chamber, we should very soon have a schedule, a timetable planning the witnesses to come in the remainder of time available to the Prosecution; that is, by the end of the Prosecution case, so that all and sundry can have an overview of the remaining witnesses. So this is a remainder for you, Mr. Scott. I believe that Mr. Mundis has already conveyed our concern to you, but this is a very major concern, and I spend every minute, every second thinking of it. We're going to have the witness brought in. Madam Usher, can you bring the witness in? Yes, Mr. Kovacic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, on Thursday at the end of the questioning of Witness Delalic, if you remember my microphone wasn't working, so I wasn't able to ask an IC number for the video, for the footage that we showed in the courtroom together with General Praljak's cross-examination. I put on the IC list which was given a number, but without the actual number. So may I have a number for that video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have the video here with me and it will become Exhibit IC 574.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, IC 574.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, sir. Let me first check that you can hear me in your own language. If you do hear me, say yes, you understand me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I understand you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, you have been called by the Prosecution as a witness in this case, which is happening currently. Please give me your first name, surname and date of birth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My first name is Philip, my surname is Watkins, and I was born on the 21st of April, 1959.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. What is your current occupation, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am chief executive of a company involved in urban regeneration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Have you had an opportunity to testify before an international court on the events that took place in the former Yugoslavia or is this going to be the first time you testify?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the third time I will have testified in this court, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So this is the third time. Can you tell us in which other cases you have been a witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was called by the Prosecution in the case of Dario Kordic, and I was called by the Defence in the case of Tihomir Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Please read out the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, sir. Please sit down. Before I give the floor to the Prosecution, I'll give you some explanation. You're used to this Tribunal since this is the first time you've testified [as interpreted]. Moreover, you were both a Prosecution and a Defence witness, which is quite something special. Therefore, you won't be surprised to the types of questions that are going to be put to you. You will first be put questions by the OTP. I guess you met with a representative of the Office of the Prosecutor this morning or yesterday, and after this first stage you have Defence teams on your left-hand side, or the accused, and they in turn will put questions to you as part of the cross-examination. The three Judges in front of you can, pursuant to the rules, intervene at any time, but for the sake of convenience and for parties to be able to present their case, we now prefer to put our questions towards the end, after the examinations by the parties, but it may happen that because of certain circumstances we might have to intervene. For instance, when some documents are being reviewed, in this instance we do have a lot of documents to go through, I think close to 54 of them, so it may be that rather than wait until the very end, in order not -- to avoid coming back to a document later on we meet intervene but only if it is absolutely necessary to do so. Try to be very specific and short in your answers. As you know, these are oral proceedings supported by documents that are going to be tendered into evidence once your testimony is over, but what matters above all is what you are going to say in answer to questions by parties. If you fail to understand a the meaning of a sentence, do not hesitate to ask the party asking you that question to reformulate it. As you know already, we have breaks for technical reasons in this Tribunal every 90 minutes, and they are about 20 minutes long. So this is very briefly the way your testimony is going to take place. If at any time you feel unwell, you want to have a break, also there again do not hesitate to say so, and I will call a break for you to have a rest, if need be. It is now your witness, Mr. Prosecutor. Mr. Registrar is going to count the time. Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Keeping with our objections in the past, we've noted that the gentleman has personal notes and used those personal notes in creating the statement that he was -- he provided to the OTP, the last one, at least. Also, he indicated that he used confidential ECMM reports. Now, he notes that he doesn't wish to turn over his personal notes, so, number one, I would like to know whether he has had a change of heart by -- since then, since making that statement, and, if so, could we have those notes. Two, if he's not willing to turn over the notes, whether he reviewed the notes prior to coming here, and also whether there are any documents that are -- that he looked at, confidential ECMM documents that are not in reference -- that are not referred to in the statement but only he had access to and the Defence has not been or the Prosecution has not had access to. So those are my questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, for several weeks already, systematically so, the Defence have been asking for documents to be turned over, notes that might have been used towards preparing a witness statement. Before you answer this question, I have to ask you this: You have already been a witness in the Kordic and in the Blaskic cases. In these both cases, did the Prosecution or the Defence ask you to turn over your personal notes or documents that you might have had access to before you wrote out or gave this written statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Both previous occasions I was asked to disclose notes which I took at the time while I was in Bosnia, and on both occasions I declined to offer those, primarily because they are a mixture of thoughts and comments after meeting individuals, but also that they contain personal information such as telephone numbers of my family and so on. So I have not disclosed those. In answer to the question pressed to me, yes, I have looked at those books prior to coming to the court today. I have not looked at any other ECMM documents except those that were presented to me in proofreading by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Second question I'd like to put: At the time you were a member of the ECMM, at the time as part of the mission you had been given specific instructions as to the documents of the ECMM, or was nothing said to the effect?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Nothing was said to the effect of -- of documents from ECMM. We were required to write daily reports. We simply wrote those and submitted them, but there was no -- no other instructions, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You heard Mr. Karnavas earlier on. You may know him already. He was officially asking for the documents to be turned over, documents that you possibly have looked at. What is your current position, faced with this request?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sir, I would not like to have hand over my notebooks. I would not like to put them in the public domain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, what is the position of the OTP on this?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Our position is the same as we've announced previously, and that is if the witness does not wish to turn over the notes, they or matter of his papers and, consistent with other Trial Chambers and other trials, the notes should not be turned over.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President, Your Honours. May I is suggest that a simple solution to all this would be to ask that the notes be turned over on a confidential basis and that any references to them during the testimony should be made in closed session, and then, obviously, if references were to be made to them in the judgement of the Trial Chamber or for other purposes, that could be done under seal. That would, I think, take care of Mr. Watkins's concern about the personal information and, at the same time, Your Honour would make available to the Defence potentially relevant information that could be important for the purposes of cross-examination. And in the exercise of Your Honours' discretion, I would submit that that is a better solution than simply denying the Defence access to potentially very helpful documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you have heard the submissions by Mr. Murphy. He suggested you would turn over the documents on a confidential basis in closed session so that it would not be disclosed to the public, and, if mentioned in the final judgement, the Judges would only refer to the notes as to the extent as they are in the public domain and not private. What do you think of this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sir, I'd rather remain consistent and not hand over the books. It may be that people perceive they will be extremely useful to either Prosecution or Defence. I think they would be very disappointed. They're merely scribblings, names, appointment next to it, a couple of thoughts. They're personal to me, and I'd rather keep it that way, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Trial Chamber has already discussed this matter. It is of the view that the documents are the private ownership of the witness, and it being so, if the witness declines to turn them over, he won't have to, all the more so, since this witness has just specified that the content of the notebooks is very personal and only personal and that in his view there would be nothing in the notebooks that might be likely to be interesting. But when they ask their questions, the Judges will be able to assess the relevance of this. But there is something else that still is not very clear. Mr. Scott, looking at the list, I realise that all the ECMM documents are in the Rule 70 column. There's a "yes" there, and until the under seal they're also mentioned as "yes" documents. Does this amount to say that the European Union told you that they didn't want the documents to be in the public domain?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. As I explained to some of your staff last week, the position of ECMM on this, as I understand it, is consistent with the position that some of the other providers such as the Spanish government and the United States have taken concerning documents produced by those providers, and that is that the documents may be referred in court. The question -- excuse me. The witness may be questioned about them, but the documents themselves will neither be broadcast or shown outside the courtroom and will be maintained in the court records under seal. That is, no member of the public would be able to either see, broadcast, or have access to the documents themselves. They may be used in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This means, doesn't it, that questions can be asked in a public fashion, and that documents will not be put on the ELMO, but the answers also will be public. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. I'm now going to give the floor to Mr. Kruger. Good afternoon, Mr. Kruger.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, everybody in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Your Honours, just at the outset I'll point out, as there have been previous witnesses who have testified regarding the structure of the ECMM as well as the reporting methods and then the structure of documents, I will not go into these details with this witness unless directly relevant regarding this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, if we may start with a few biographical details. Could you please tell the Court what your background was prior to becoming an ECMM monitor.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I studied economics and politics and achieved a degree, a bachelor of honours degree and then a Master of Science at the London School of Economics. I worked for a while on the family farm before joining the British Army, where I served after training at Sandhurst as an officer in the royal artillery and the royal horse artillery. I left the military forces and was recruited by the Foreign and Commonwealth Office to act as an observer seconded to the European Community Monitor Mission. I served between 1993 and 1995 in Bosnia and in Croatia. I then joined the political staff of Mr. Yasushi Akashi, the Special Representative to the Secretary-General of the United Nations and worked for four months with him in 1995 in Zagreb. I then left the employ of the -- of international organisations and established a company along with some colleagues. That was involved in trying to get companies rebuilding Bosnia following the Dayton peace agreement. That company was in existence for three years, and I then was approached by the Foreign and Commonwealth Office and asked if I would join a new international verification mission which was being established in Kosovo. I joined that mission before the NATO intervention in Kosovo, and then after the NATO intervention in Kosovo I stayed with the Organisation of Security and Cooperation in Europe and worked specialising in elections, and was involved in the municipal elections and subsequent elections in Kosovo. I then returned to the United Kingdom, and for the last five years I've been involved in trying to bring new investment into deprived areas within British towns where there is particular deprivation. That is the occupation I have now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, how many years did you spend in the British military?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: Eight years.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And of those eight years how -- how much of those years were spent as an artillery officer or involved with artillery?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: I spent one year of training at Sandhurst and then I specialised special to arms training at the Royal School of Artillery, and so for the remaining seven years. I first served with air defence artillery, our surface to air missiles and then was a forward observer with traditional artillery for another three years.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you. Turning to your time in Bosnia, you said that you were there as a monitor between 1993 and 1995. Could you give us the breakdowns of in which areas you worked during which periods?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: I first deployed to the ECMM mission in late January 1993, and after a brief induction in Zagreb I deployed to Bosnia where I served as a member of a team in Tomislavgrad but spent most of my time in Gornji Vakuf. By June of 1993, I was appointed as the head of the coordination centre, so in charge of several times in Travnik covering an area of Central Bosnia, and I held that position through to October 1993, where I transferred to Mostar as the head of the coordination centre in Mostar, and I remained there until -- I think it was early January 1994. I was then required by my government to spend three months back in the UK, but was then sent back to the ECMM mission, and I served for approximately two months, maybe three, in Croatia as the head of the coordination centre for the ECMM in Topusko, working in the Krajina area. I was then appointed as the head of the Regional Centre Zenica, which later changed its name during my period to Regional Centre BiH, and I was responsible for running all of the ECMM teams in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you. Just for clarity, coordination centre, for instance, Coordination Centre Travnik, is that abbreviated as CC Travnik in correspondence?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: Yes. CC Travnik or CC Mostar or CC Tapusko.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, sir, just looking at the various levels at which you worked, as an ECMM team member attached to CC Gornji Vakuf, at what level were your contacts?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: Primarily at a brigade level, but one rapidly began to work with more senior individuals. So in Gornji Vakuf, within four or five weeks of arrival, I was dealing with the operational zone commander, Colonel Siljeg, and of the armija forces with commander of 4th Corps, General Arif Pasalic, and also members of 3rd Corps, senior members of 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you. And what -- where -- or was your focus when you became head of a coordination centre?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: The geographical area became wider. As a team member, as I noted, the title of my team was "Tomislavgrad," but because of the nature of activities in the areas where we needed to concentrate, I actually spent most of my time in Gornji Vakuf, and in that capacity would have a responsibility running from Bugojno down through Prozor to Jablanica. As the head of the coordination centre in Travnik, I was responsible for an area which included that valley, the Vrbas valley, but also the Lasva Valley, and then Zenica and as far to the north-east as Zepce and Zavidovici and Vares. My responsibilities ended at the point at which CC Travnik and -- sorry, CC Tuzla and the head Tuzla's area, so they covered the -- up to the Posavina Corridor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: During your period in 1993, 1994 as an ECMM monitor, was your efforts focused on any specific ethnic groupings and relations or events between them?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: Primarily I was dealing with relations between the Bosnian Croats and the Bosnian Muslims. I had very little contact with the Bosnian Serbs, although there were one or two meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, when you became head of a -- of CC Mostar, Coordination Centre Mostar, could you very briefly just tell the Court where your focus of contact was during that period?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: Well, by this time, because of the fact I had been in the country and working continuously for approximately nine months, I had gained a lot of experience and was primarily dealing with the senior leadership of the Bosnian Croats, and that would include some of the defendants here today. Mr. Prlic was an interlocutor, as indeed were several others here today.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, sir, at this stage I'd just like to very briefly refer you to document 4106. Now, document 4106, or Exhibit 4106 appears to be a daily summary report dated 10 August 1993, from team V to CC Travnik to RC Zenica. My first question to you, sir, is: Do you recognise this report?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: Can I just clarify? Mine says 11th of August rather than the 10th.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sorry, the 11th of August. That's my mistake.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: This is a report that would have been sent from the headquarters of the Travnik coordination centre to the regional centre in Zenica, and this is a report which I wrote.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, sir, if you could look at the second page of the report, and that would be paragraph 8, which says "Assessment" right at the end. Now, in that assessment it states that the emphasis in CC Travnik remains on humanitarian work," and then it goes on to state some other things, but then it says: "It is ironic that access to the Croat community is normally uninhibited but access to the Muslim minorities such as Prozor remains difficult". Now, my question to you, perhaps in the context of this, but you may go wider, is while you were a monitor, an ECMM monitor during 1993, 1994, did you have any problems gaining access to the areas you were supposed to monitor?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: Yes. We had considerable access, and we were blocked from visiting isolated Muslim communities, but equally often blocked from visiting isolated Croatian communities. It was a consistent factor in our operations, and we needed to address these by going to the senior levels to try and get access.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Was the issue of access ever fully resolved?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: No. There was often temporarily a breakthrough, an agreement and overcoming of the immediate issue but it would inevitably return at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, if we can just very briefly look at your time as -- with the team in CC Gornji Vakuf. What was your primary task or focus when you were in Gornji Vakuf on the ECMM team?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: A joint commission had been established prior to my arrival, which was a commission formed of representatives of the HVO and of the armija, and the idea was to try and introduce and build confidence where there had been some early conflict in January, and the sort of activity we were engaged in was, first of all, discussions, separation of forces, removal of trenches, agreement on where flags could be flown or not flown, and then vir if I case by actually physically going to these areas to assure what had been agreed around the table was actually happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: From the Bosnian Croat side or the HVO side, do you know who had been involved in the setting up of this joint commission?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: Yes. It was established at a very senior level, and I believe that initially it was established at a level which involved General Petkovic. By the time I was there, I was dealing with General Siljeg and Arif Pasalic, as mentioned earlier. So having been established, it was then the local military or the corps commanders and operational zone commanders we were dealing with, as well as the subservient brigades to those organisations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: From the ECMM side who chaired this meeting?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: When I first arrived it was being chaired by an Irish monitor called Ray Lane. It -- on his departure - I don't remember the exact date, but it was fairly early on; I would say in February - he was succeeded by a British monitor called Christopher Beese, and in either of those absence then, the team itself would chair, and so on occasions I chaired those meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you. You've mentioned Christopher Beese and Mr. Ray Lane. Could I ask you, when you arrived in Bosnia, how did you come up to speed or gain your knowledge in -- sufficient knowledge to be able to function?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: We had an initial brief in -- in Zagreb, just an orientation, a very general brief. Then arriving in -- in Bosnia, we had one-to-one discussions with monitors who had been there that much longer, including the two people you mention, but also your immediate team leader who would have more experience. So it was really a case of that direct communication through those individuals. You had reference to some of the reports that had been previously written, but the biggest experience was the experience you gained rapidly in those -- in those situations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, sir, if I could refer you to Exhibit 5502. Exhibit 5502. And this is an ECMM report dated 30 September 1993, issued by team V2 in Gornji Vakuf addressed to CC Travnik. And, sir, if I -- first of all, could I ask you, do you have any -- do you know about this document or could you tell us where this document comes from, what it is?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: Yes. This would be a -- a report written at a team level, sent to the coordination centre, and it's giving a background of the municipalities of Gornji Vakuf. And the reason for this was because there was a rapid turnover of monitors, some serving for as little as six weeks in the case of the Belgium monitors, most serving for three months, a few such as the British monitors serving for a year, we found those that had been there any time wanting to get some corporate knowledge and understanding. So we asked teams to draw up briefs, some background reports to help make it easy for new arrivals to understand the patch, and this is one of those reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, if I may refer you specifically to paragraph 2, which is "History of the area." And this paragraph, it basically gives a summary of events in Gornji Vakuf from the beginning of 1993, and it goes on to say that Gornji Vakuf was the focus of HVO policy in the region and direction came from corps HQ in Mostar. The next paragraph on 8 January 1993, "an HVO flag was raid in the town of Gornji Vakuf," et cetera. Now, do you recall having been shown this paragraph during our meeting prior to -- to testifying, or one of our meetings prior to testifying?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And are you able to comment on -- on this reflection of the history of that area?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: Well, it is a -- a very brief summary which would introduce a new monitor to some of the structures that were in place and the importance that Gornji Vakuf had. By the time this report was written on the 30th of September, 1993, the events and focus of activity was elsewhere, but Gornji Vakuf in January 1993 had been one of the key focuses. So it would be a useful introduction but not massively comprehensive.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Okay. Two-thirds of the way down in that paragraph it states: "A joint commission was established to deal with extant issues and later humanitarian agencies were involved." Is this joint commission the one which you were involved with and to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, that joint commission, did it continue working through 1993?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: Yes, but I would say that it had probably reached its peak of -- of influence in February, March, 1993, because by April we had a very different military situation, and although -- in that area, particularly in Central Bosnia. So although the functions of the ECMM in trying to keep discussions going between Bosnian Croats and Muslims would have been there, the joint commission as such would have had evaporated after April.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: The beginning of the last paragraph -- well, just beneath that section that I've just read on page 1, it says: "Since June of 1993, the situation in Gornji Vakuf has reduced to one of open warfare." Is that pretty much as you recall what happened?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: I may not have used the word "open warfare" myself. I mean, what had -- Gornji Vakuf was an important town on a front line, and it was important because of its control of access routes further into Bosnia. Open warfare, well, it wasn't an intense front line, although there was military activity there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, sir, in June 1993, you said that you then moved to CC Travnik. At the time of your move, who was the head of CC Travnik?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: The head of CC Travnik was a Swedish monitor whose name just momentarily escapes me. A Swedish fighter pilot. I --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Did you replace him after a short while as head?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: Yes. He was there for a matter of a week or -- or two weeks and then left.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: The headquarters of CC Travnik, where was that? Was it in Travnik itself?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: Yes, it was. We actually established a headquarters in the -- in a hotel in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And did it remain there?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: No, it didn't. Shortly after we'd opened it, the fighting between the Croats and Muslims intensified in -- in April, and we were evacuated when there was fighting in that town, and so we operated still with the name of CC Travnik, but by -- I can't remember the exact date we were evacuated, but sometime in late April we were then based in Zenica, operating out of Zenica, covering the same territorial area but not physically located in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, CC Travnik, is it correct that that also felt -- fell under the regional centre or RC Zenica?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: During June what was the organisation of RC Zenica? Along what lines was it organised?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: It's -- RC Zenica had formed in early January and had grown out of Split in Croatia. It had been planted in Zenica, and it was organised primarily as a mechanism for helping to introduce the Vance-Owen Peace Plan, which was the main international reconciliation effort, and we on the ground were tasked with preparing and supporting and trying to build confidence in institutions, and so teams began to focus very specifically on making connections with the political community and -- and trying to send information back up to Vance -- Cyrus Vance and Lord Owen on what the feeling was on the ground and how real it was to implement this -- this plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And did this organisation then change the organisation along the lines of the Vance-Owen Peace Plan for RC Zenica?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: The geographical areas changed a little bit. One example would be the time that was working in Gornji Vakuf. When that -- I was in that team in January. It reported to Mostar. What was then CC Grude, which became CC Mostar. But during this period it reconfigured and reported to CC Travnik. So although the Vance-Owen Plan very clearly was not going to be a success by the early summer of 1993, the teams essentially covered the same sort of territory, but the activity was different. It was much more about fire-fighting-type duties, humanitarian, organising temporary cease-fires, exchange of prisoners, bodies, visiting isolated communities, trying to let them know that they weren't forgotten.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now, from there, in October you then became head of CC Mostar. Who had been your predecessor as head of CC Mostar?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: Martin Garrod, Sir Martin Garrod.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: When you arrived did you immediately assume the duty of -- actually I see you want to add something?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: Yes. Actually he had been the head of CC Mostar, but he was replaced by a Spanish monitor called Jesus Amatriain, and Sir Martin Garrod became the head of the regional centre. So he asked me to go to Mostar, and I then reported to him as the head of the regional centre but I took over from Jesus Amatriain.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Was there an overlap period between you and Jesus Amatriain?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: Yes, a short period. I forget exactly but, again, it would have been somewhere around a week.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Okay. Whom did Sir Martin Garrod replace as head of RC Zenica?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: Jean-Pierre Thebault, a French monitor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, when you arrived in Mostar, what was the actual level that you were conducting your contacts at? Actually, I have asked you that. Sorry. I will ask you this, though: How would you describe the people you were dealing with when you became head of CC Mostar?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: Well, the aim was to get the highest possible access you could so I strove to meet the senior political and military leaders.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, before moving into some more detail regarding that, could you tell or give the Court an idea of what were the main issues which were -- or which were playing during October, November, December 1993 in Mostar when you were there?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: In Mostar on the humanitarian side it was discussions and activity around evacuation of hospitals, exchange of prisoners, and freedom of movement for humanitarian aid. On the political side, it was the development of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna having earlier - I think in August 1993 - changed from the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna to the Croatian republic. Institutions were forming, and that was a particular it interest to the European Community Monitor Mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned humanitarian issues, exchanges, et cetera. Was there any particular exchange which was particularly high profile during this period, which caused a -- which drew a lot of attention?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: I would say there were two. The first I was immediately involved with was the attempt to evacuate the hospital in East Mostar in conjunction with a similar evacuation of a hospital in Central Bosnia, Nova Bila, and essentially the idea was that there would be simultaneous evacuation of the hospital. The one from Central Bosnia would be evacuated by helicopter, while the one from East Mostar would be a land escort, and I was involved in East Mostar at the hospital trying to get that element of the -- of the operation functioning. That actually collapsed when the helicopters that flew out of Nova Bila landed in -- I forget exactly where they did land. It will probably come to me, but certainly in Herzegovinian territory and were -- were seized, and that prevented the evacuation of East Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: By whom were these helicopters seized?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: Well, we were told that they were seized by families, by civilian population, but it was very evident that, had there been a will to actually allow those helicopters to fly again, that could have been achieved. So it was a convenient -- a convenient explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: If you say they were seized by people, and -- did these people belong to any group?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: They were Bosnian Croats, but I have no doubt that they were being instructed and hadn't -- hadn't themselves of their own volition decided to stop the helicopters taking off.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: We will -- this issue of the helicopters will come up in a number of documents that we deal with, but could I ask you at this stage, how long did it take to solve this issue?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: I was dealing with the helicopters certainly until I left, which was in early -- I think it was early February 1994, and I don't believe it was resolved in that period. So a period of three or four months.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: I see that you wanted to add something.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: Yes. There were two main humanitarian issues. That was one, and the second one was about the release of prisoners of -- of war and exchanges where there had been several attempts, but there was an announcement in early December 1993 by Mate Boban that he was going to release prisoners. So that was another main area that we were dealing with.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: During your period in Mostar, that was when the Old Bridge or Stari Most was also destroyed. Was this at all an issue which the ECMM also took an interest?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: Yes, it was an issue we took an interest in.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And did you get -- come to hear or know about the Stupni Do incident during this period that you were there?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: Yes. Stupni Do happened just after I'd left Central Bosnia. It had fallen into my area of responsibility, but I then -- my understanding what happened at Stupni Do came from the successor monitors up in Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, sir in the course of further -- of the further examination a number of these issues will come up in various documents, sometimes in combination, sometimes singly, and so we will be touching upon a number of these issues as we go along. Now, returning to your contacts, and if I may focus specifically on your contacts as head of CC Mostar with Bosnian Croat leadership. Could you perhaps briefly, first, just describe or mention who were the people that you met with, the main people?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: I met with a -- a broad group, but my primary interface at a senior level was with Jadranko Prlic. I also met with Mr. Pusic, who was the head of all dealings with regard to prisoner exchanges. I dealt and met with some of the Presidency advisors who were forming a new Presidency circle around Mate Boban. I met Mate Boban himself. And Vladislav Pogarcic would be one of the examples of the people I met, and I also met many of the mayors and senior leaders. So Ivan Bender from Neum, and Mr. Tokic from Tomislavgrad, and other key leaders.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Okay. The -- focusing for a moment on the accused in this case, did you meet with Bruno Stojic at any stage?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: I don't remember meeting him, although we regularly met with his deputy, Slobodan Bozic. I simply don't remember having a direct meeting with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And what about General Praljak?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: Yes, I met General Praljak on a number of occasions, but actually primarily when I was the head of CC Travnik, and I met him in Prozor and near Prozor on the front line at the Makljen ridge. And I tried to meet him in Citluk, which is the headquarters of the HVO -- actually, to address a number of the issues we've touched upon, by then there was uncertainty as to who was the commander-in-chief of the HVO forces. First of all, there had been some uncertainty as to the exact point at which General Petkovic departed and General Praljak turned over, and again between General Praljak and the arrival of Ante Roso. But I met all of these military leaders and including others such as -- operational zone commander was Colonel Lasic, and General Tole, who I met.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Valentin Coric, did you ever meet with Valentin Coric?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: The name is very familiar and was right from the beginning. It was a name of somebody who Ray Lane in particular seemed to meet. He was the commander of the military police. I may have met him, but again, perhaps in retrospect, one wonders why I didn't, but I don't remember actually meeting him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, if we may turn specifically then to Mr. Jadranko Prlic. When was the first time that you actually did meet with Jadranko Prlic?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: I believe that I met him in the very first few weeks when I visited Mostar, because my team reported to Mostar, and I met Ray Lane. The reason there is a hesitation is, in the early days and I'm sure you would appreciate, in a complex environment with many names it took a few weeks, a few months to begin to understand who was who. But -- I believe I met him there, but the first time I certainly met him and had a good working relationship with him was when I became head of CC Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Just to be clear, when you say the first time you met him was in the very few -- first few weeks, would that be the very first weeks that you actually went to Bosnia as an ECMM monitor?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: Yes. This would have been February or early March 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: At that stage, could you give the Court an idea of your awareness of what position he held or his status?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: I was told that he was the Prime Minister of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, from October onwards when you became head of CC Mostar, where did you meet generally with Jadranko Prlic?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: I met him in West Mostar in his office, but that wasn't the only time I met him. There was an odd -- a couple of social occasions. I went to a Christmas gathering of senior leaders, and I was also hosted by Mr. Prlic when I brought the ambassador, the head of the mission, the whole of the ECMM mission, from Zagreb. He hosted me at -- primarily it was meetings in his office. One other meeting I had with him was when he invited me to go to the first presidential or -- sorry, not -- the first convening of the government of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna. I'd established a good relationship with Mr. Prlic. I found him very easy to talk to and he was always very open, and he was keen that the European Community heard the voice of -- of the Croatian -- Bosnian Croats, and so he -- he invited me to this session at the end of December 1993. So various locations, primarily his office.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Okay. Just before we have a look at another document, you said you met him in the -- in his office in Mostar. Could you give the Court an idea of whether the Ministry of Defence may also have been housed in this location or not?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: Actually, I think the Ministry of Defence was in a separate building, although I can't be absolutely sure. Certainly I met other -- other lead -- political leaders in the same offices as Mr. Prlic, but I believe that when I saw Slobodan Bozic and went to see Mr. Stojic, it was in another building.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Okay. Sir, if I may refer you to document 6084. Exhibit 6084. And this is an ECMM daily summary from CC Mostar dated 25 October 1993. Do you recognise this -- this document?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: Yes. I wrote this document, and I note that on that date, 25th, I'm still signing myself as "Des," which means the designate. So I can't remember the exact date I arrived in Mostar. I think it was about 17 or 18th of October, and so a week later I'm still the Des. So Jesus Amatriain would also have been in territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: So if we look at the very first paragraph on -- the first paragraph under "Political" on page 1, it starts off with "HCC and HCC (Des)." So does that refer then to you as HCC Des?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: HCC would be Jesus Amatriain, and I would be HCC Des.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, if we can look on page 1, the is second paragraph under "Political." It's about the middle of the page, and it says that, "HCC and HCC (Des) met Jadranko Prlic and the situation of Croats in Central Bosnia as the main topic and previous experience on the area proved an asset." Was this the first meeting that you had, well, as -- when you went to Mostar as head of CC Mostar?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: Yes, I believe it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And can you comment on -- on this, on this meeting?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: Yes. I suppose it established the beginning of -- of the relationship I've described of one of -- of easy access and open discussion. The reason I make a comment here about my experience in Central Bosnia is because we -- there was a physical separation between Herzegovina and Mostar and the activities that were happening in, for instance, the -- in the Lasva Valley, and because of the position I'd had before dealing with everything up as far as Vares and Zavidovici and Zepce, I believe that my -- my understanding of the position of the isolated Bosnian Croat communities in Central Bosnia was of particular interest to Mr. Prlic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: The very next paragraph -- my apologies. The very next paragraph refers to 5.000 refugees who had arrived in Herzegovina last week and a further 10.000 were expected during the next two months, and the comment which is added states that: "The figure of 5.000 was also quoted by Jadranko Prlic, who added that accompanying them were -- or accommodating them would now be a serious concern." Could you comment on this?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: Yes. This was a time of particularly large movements of population from Central Bosnia. Bosnian Croats coming out of Central Bosnia through Bosnian Serb territory and re-entering into Bosnian Croat territory around Herzegovina. There were primarily two locations this happened. Celebici to the north of Mostar up on the front line, and also Stolac, which was to the south-west of -- of Mostar. And these were the points at which civilians came out of Central Bosnia and re-entered into Herzegovina. And so any movements were of -- of this sort of scale were interesting on a number of fronts. Just the sheer scale, the humanitarian issues that were raised as are mentioned here, but also the cooperation that must signal between the Bosnian Croats and the Bosnian Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, sir, if we can perhaps just turn to the next page of that document. "Other matters," which is paragraph 6, and the very first paragraph there states is that "HCC Des," which would have been you, "contacted by telephone Vladislav Pogarcic," and this was in regard to the question of the hijacked helicopters. And it says, "As a result of this information, HCC and HCC Des have arranged a meeting with General Tole for 26 October. General Praljak was not available." Could you comment on this?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: Yes. First of all Vladislav Pogarcic was one of the main people that I met. He was forming or was an advisor to Mate Boban and giving me a very, again, open discussions about the Presidency and how that was formed. The reason I was raising the helicopters is for those already discussed. The continued holding of the helicopters was preventing further evacuations in and exchanges and indeed general cooperation between the Bosnian Croats and the Bosnian Muslims and we wanted to take it out as an issue, and I obviously saw General Praljak still as the important person to meet in terms of military, being the commander of -- of HVO. But that suggested saying he wasn't available. I don't think at this stage raised any particular issues but it was in this particular period we were unsure quite who was in command where.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, if we can step off that document. You've already mentioned that you had a favourable impression of Mr. Prlic. From -- from your dealings with him, could you comment on whether he possessed or what the authority was that he possessed, if any?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: Well, he was the Prime Minister of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, so he was in a very senior position. We were seeing a formation of the Presidency, the government, and the parliament, and he was obviously a key player, certainly at the government level. He spoke English. He was the same age as me, similar background in terms of economics, and, as I said, we -- I found him very approachable and open to discussion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Did you ever discuss him with other people, with other leadership figures or internationals?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: Yes. He would have been, and was indeed an important person in terms of any visitors we had, international visitors. I hosted a visitor of Ambassador de Baenst, the Belgium head of mission, and I took him to see Mr. Prlic. Mr. Prlic was involved in certain discussions as we approached things like the -- the discussions in Geneva and discussions in Washington. He wasn't necessarily the person that went there, but he was certainly someone we wanted to -- to talk with, to get our -- an understanding of the Bosnian Croat perspective.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, on the question of authority, which we've touched upon, to your mind when you were down there, did you have the impression that he could actually exert authority?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: Yes. He was in a position of authority. What became increasingly apparent to me, though, was trying to understand the relationship between the government and the Presidency, and there were many discussions and uncertainties as to who as persons were in the ascendance and who perhaps was disappearing off the scene, and that was both in the military and on the political side. Mr. Prlic I didn't ever get any impression that his position was in any way threatened, but I was interested, for instance, in -- in views about other government positions and who was going to fill them, and I found Mr. Prlic was always quite open and -- and informative.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: When you referred to the Presidency just a few lines up and the relationship between the government and the Presidency, which is on line 2 of page 32, the Presidency, to whom are you referring to or what are you referring to there?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, could you just point me to the document?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sorry, it's on the transcript. You stated that you were trying to understand the relationship between the government and the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: Yes. The Presidency was Mate Boban, and there were many discussions and many rumours that Mate Boban was on the way out as -- as the political -- the main political character for the Bosnian Croats. The information we were receiving from discussions with senior Bosnian Croat leaders in Central Bosnia, but also from discussions that I was having, his position was uncertain. But that's what I mean by his presence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, perhaps could you give the Court an indication of the issues that you were discussing with Jadranko Prlic in your time as head of CC Mostar?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: I primarily spoke to him about the political institutions of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, which would have included some discussion about the military structures but primarily it was about who was going to be the new Minister of Justice, the international relations minister, and so on, and these power struggles. I did speak to him about issues of humanitarian aid, but those would have been primarily dealt with by Mr. Pusic, and later a humanitarian organisation was formed that was led by Martin Raguz, and we did a lot of the humanitarian discussions with -- with him had.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Okay. Did you ever discuss with Mr. Prlic his views on the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna and its role?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: What were his views on that?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: The Croatian -- the establishment of the Croatian republic was seen as an important signal to be sent not only to the Croatian Community but to other ethnic groups within Bosnia and indeed to the international community. It was the movement from the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, gathering of interests and important aspects of the Croatian in -- of the Croatian Community into -- into a much more governmental structure, something with an equivalence which was mentioned sever times to the self-styled republic which the Bosnian Serbs had set up. It was a step and a demonstration of a self-styled state that he wished to see recognised, certainly at an international level, and it seemed to be a move towards some sort of tri-republic solution. This is before the Federation and the ideas that were emerging were one of Bosnia remaining within its existing borders but with three republics, and there was much discussion about aspects of that, but the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, its state organisations, its functions, its legality, its relationship with the military structures, that was my primary discussions with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: How would you assess his role during October, November, December in actually setting up the government of this Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna? Did he have an important role there or not?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: Yes, he did. He was due to form the government, and the government was then to be presented to the parliament, and the parliament would ratify it. At least that's ostensibly what was happening. What was of interest to us was, who had the final say? Was it Mr. Prlic or was it Mr. Boban? What was the relationship there? Was it going to be presented to the parliament and merely rubber-stamped or was there any challenge to what was being represented?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Okay. Just prior to stepping onto the next document which will build on what we've just been talking about I would just like to refer back to one specific thing you mentioned that you said regarding humanitarian matters, you actually more often referred to where you had to go to Mr. Pusic, but just generally on this, did -- was Mr. Prlic well-informed about these humanitarian matters and exchange issues, to your mind?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: Yes, I think he was informed, although it was -- his interest was primarily in these political structures I saw, and I was indeed referred to other people to sort out those issues. So I think there was knowledge, but a distancing and a focus of interest on political structures.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, sir, if we can step on or continue. You mentioned earlier a meeting by the head of mission of the ECMM, and I'd like to quickly or -- deal with this now. First of all, in October, towards the end of October, who was or became the head of mission of the ECMM?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: At that time it was Ambassador de Baenst.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Was he from Belgium?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: From Belgium. If it helps, the head of mission changed with the rotations of the EU Presidency. So you see the change each time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Okay. And is it correct that the Belgian ambassador then did come down to visit various leadership figures in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: Yes. He came on quite an extensive visit, and he met Radovan Karadzic. He met Izetbegovic. I think Haris Silajdzic, Ganic, and then he came into Mostar, which is my area in terms of organising, and I took him to see Mate Boban, Mr. Prlic. I think Slobodan Bozic was also at that -- at that meeting. Yes, he was. And then I took him to East Mostar where we met the new 4th Corps commander of the armija, who was General Budakovic. And we also met Smejl Klaric [phoen] and Ibrahim Kaluda who were the civilian leaders in East Mostar at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: If I can refer you to Exhibit 06693. Exhibit 6693. And this is title "Special report number one." It's an ECMM document from the ECMM liaison officer to ICFY, Elmar Dinter. Is this a report on the meeting of the head of mission, the Belgian ambassador?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: Yes. It's notable for being -- handwritten is unusual for an ECMM, but it may be just a fax cover.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, if we can look at the third page of the document, and there is a list of people met, and towards the end, the third last name is Mate Boban. The second last name, Jadranko Prlic, and then Arif Pasalic, and the date is then given for all these, the 30th of October. Do you have that?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: These meetings, it states that they took place in Grude, Mostar west bank, and then Mostar east bank. So is it correct that these were three separate meetings?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: Yes, three separate meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, sir, if I may refer you to the page of the report which, if you see at the top of the report there's number DK00. If you could look at the one which says 7227. DK007227. Do you have that?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Toward -- two-thirds down the page there's C and then "the Croat objectives." And what this paragraph then states is that all Croat interlocutors want a solution with ethnic partition, and essentially Mr. Boban wants immediate negotiations while Kordic and Prlic feel it is too early. Could you comment on this paragraph?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: Well, first I would say two things. I didn't write it. It's not one of my reports. And the second thing is just a point. I believe that we met General Budakovic rather than Pasalic, but those we may be able to verify that with another report. Now specifically here --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I could interrupt for a second, sir. I will raise an objection at this point, and I didn't do so earlier. I thought that the gentleman would have been familiar with this report but it's obvious that there was a foundation that was lacking in this case. Since the gentleman did not generate this report, I would object to the gentleman commenting on what somebody else might have opined on. If the gentleman has an opinion of his own that he wishes to share, keeping in mind that he had just arrived in the area only shortly before this time in Mostar - we're talking about October, as I understand it he had just come into the Mostar area - I think that he may not be in the best position to be opining as to what somebody else's opinion might have been.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will try and rectify that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Is -- sir, first of all could you comment on the origins of this document?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: Well, it's come from an ECMM liaison officer. On the 16th of November I'd been there for a month, and that was after 10 months in Bosnia. So I think I would have picked things up pretty quickly. And while I appreciate what's just been said, I was at those meetings so I am able to say what I think happened there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Can you comment on what happened to the meeting, whether this issue was discussed and in what context? And I'm now referring to the view that Boban wants negotiation, Prlic and Kordic feel it may be too early. If you can recall that.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: The timing of this particular visit was at a time when we were looking at an international level for the solution, but this is before the announcement of the Federation. So we were very interested in everyone's perspective on the future, and certainly it was stated by Mate Boban that he was ready for immediate resumption. I think the general consistent pattern that we saw was that at that stage the solution seemed to be three republics. There were issues about how the Muslims would get to the sea and that became important, but here, that Kordic -- I wasn't at the meeting with Kordic, believe it's too early, I -- I would be speculating as to why they thought it was too early. I don't recall exactly what was said, but of course this was the period at which they were just forge the institutions of the Croatian republic. So he was just or about to present the government to the parliament. The parliament hadn't met because that happened at the end of December, so the structures that would send a signal to the international community about there being a viable interlocutor, a viable state with which one could have discussions, that wasn't quite there yet. You know, give it a couple of months and there would be more legitimacy because the process would have gone through than would exist here at this time in November.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I see it's nearly a quarter to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Before we break, Your Honour, just one clarification. Is the gentleman suggesting now that from his recollection, after meeting Prlic, Prlic indeed was of the position that it was too early for a negotiated solution, because he said that he wasn't at the meeting with Kordic, and then he gave his explanation and he gave a reason behind the explanation but the question now is whether Prlic himself to his understanding, to his knowledge, to his belief --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, we believe that you will be in a position to ask these questions during your cross-examination. Please do not interrupt the examination-in-chief for such questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well. I just -- well, the objection then would be non-responsive to the question that was asked by the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's a quarter to 4.00. We'll have a 20-minute break and resume at five past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The hearing is resume. You have the floor, Mr. Kruger.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, during the break I've been informed by the interpreters that they've requested that we make a break between question and answer just to help them with the interpretation. It was mostly my fault, I suspect. Sir, if we -- we're still busy with document 06693, and if I can refer you to the same paragraph C, the Croat objectives. That's where we were last. Now, if we -- if you turn the page; the report then goes further: "When talking about the Stupni Do massacre, Prlic, who condemned the incident, mentioned that they had not been up there," and it actually goes further because this is raised again further on the -- in the report, and that is if you go to -- if you page two pages further, and this is the page which reads at the top DK007230. Point H is the Stupni Do massacre, and the second paragraph in that is: "In fact, the only -- only the Croat Prlic condemn the action, while Boban and Kordic tended to play down the seriousness of the Stupni Do. They seemed, however, well aware of the negative effect it exerts through the media." Sir, do you recall the issue of Stupni Do being raised during your meetings with Mate Boban, and then with Jadranko Prlic on the 30th of October?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And can you tell the Court basically what the views were expressed by Boban and then by Mr. Prlic?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: Yes. Stupni Do, it happened a matter of a -- a few days before this meeting, and a -- a confused picture had first emerged as to what had happened, but all the reports coming back from both the UN and ECMM were giving a very clear indication that it was an atrocity committed by Bosnian Croat forces, and I think very quickly in our discussions -- first of all Bosnian Croat leaders in -- in the Herzegovina area were interested in what had happened. There was no doubt that this was a serious international incident, and there were various degrees of explanation offered from, "It was nothing to do with us," to, I think, the most senior leadership as exhibited by Prlic, a realisation in fact that it was Bosnian Croat forces that had committed that, and an open admittance of from Mr. Prlic, whereas certainly Mr. Mate Boban, and it appears from the meeting that was also the same view offered by Dario Kordic, it was very much played down. I think this is important for another reason. I think one of the reasons why Mr. Prlic was willing to engage with us was very much an attempt to get the Bosnian Croat voice heard and a recognition of how important it was that they went on a sort of a -- a media offensive to present themselves in a better light than they were getting reported by the international community. It was a consistent refrain from Bosnian Croat leaders that the EU and the UN only listened to and only accepted the Muslim perspective and not theirs. And there were another -- one or two other characters. I think we've mentioned Vladislav Pogarcic and another was Mile Akmadzic, who were much more aware of the importance of the international perspective, and here we note that the different attitudes, but also they were very well aware that at this moment when they were trying to send signals and trying to be taken more seriously by the international community, they were also -- that here was another event which put them in a bad light.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, if we can return to section C, two pages earlier again. And this is the page marked DK007228. And just after the part which we'd previously read on Stupni Do, it says: "The incapacity," that's four lines down, "the incapacity of Herzegovinian Croats to release the two BiH medevac helicopters," and so there once again the medevac helicopters was discussed. Could I just ask you, was this issue raised during your meetings with Mr. Boban and with Mr. Prlic?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: It was certainly raised with Mr. Boban. I actually don't remember whether we raised it with Mr. Prlic. I think it's highly likely we did, but I can't be sure on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, if I may refer you to the -- the final part of that paragraph, and here is an assessment, and I want to ask you whether you share this assessment or have a different view, the -- dealing with the failure to release the medevac helicopters shows either that the command structure in Herzegovina is not reliable or that the Herzegovinian Croats attach more importance to the release of prisoners of war in Mostar, East Mostar, than to the long overdue evacuation of wounded and sick from the Travnik-Busovaca pocket.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: Could I just take a moment to actually read the whole paragraph just to then --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: Thank you. There were complex and interlinked relations between movement of humanitarian aid, evacuation of -- of prisoners, and -- sorry, evacuation of hospitals and prisoner exchanges, and at any one moment each one of those may have more -- be attributed more importance than another, and I think here there's some speculations as to the motives of why won't the Bosnian Croats release those helicopters? And there were some very simple explanations offered at the time. This was 50 per cent of the armija's air force caught, and why release and relinquish an important logistical support? That's a very pure military aspect. Another one was about the leverage it gave for negotiations, be it prisoner of war exchange or -- or some other evacuation. So I think also within that are discussions, obviously, about the relationship between what was happening in Herzegovina and the leadership in -- in Central Bosnia. We were always very interested to know whether there was difference of views and difference of emphasis, but I can throw no more light than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Okay. Before stepping off the helicopter issue, if you turn the page and you go to section G, which is medical evacuation and release of prisoners of war, and you actually turn the next page, it's then the third paragraph of this section but the top of the page marked DK007230. This says: "Although Boban promised us on 30 October he would do his utmost to get the helicopters released (I will go there myself if Minister Stojic cannot do the job. Nothing of the sort happened)." Can you recall whether any incident or discussion to this effect during the meeting?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. Mate Boban was in full flow. He was talking expansively about the Bosnian Croat perspective in his view, and I remember him saying this, you know, quite dramatically, "I will go there myself and sort it out," but interestingly pointing to Minister of Defence Mr. Stojic as his responsibility first. So, yes, I'll do something about it, but actually somebody else is responsible for holding those. In fact, we tried political, military, and we could not get those helicopters released.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, finally on this document, if you could go to section E, which is on page DK007228. And this is the section dealing with ECMM and EC, and the second paragraph is the one which says: "Pogarcic and Prlic expressed their good relations with ECMM, although hint that the results are meager, while Prlic indirectly criticises," and then it says, "Boban and Pogarcic are less diplomatic," a few lines down. Did the issue -- do you recall the issue of the relations with the ECMM and the attitude of the ECMM coming up during the meetings with Prlic?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I think, as I said earlier, Prlic was astute to the need to send good signals, and in fact we did have good relationships with, broadly speaking, Mr. Pogarcic and Mr. Prlic, but the EC and UN were constantly being blamed by both factions for either failing to solve the issues or, in fact, indeed, in causing them in the first place. And what we're teasing out here is a difference of emphasis with Boban and Pogarcic speaking more directly and Mr. Prlic giving a -- perhaps a more measured support for ECMM, though hinting that not everything was good for the ECMM or EU generally.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, from your experience and your time down there, was this justified, this criticism, in your mind?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: No. I think it was part of the rich tapestry of pointing the blame anywhere other than where it sat.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Actually, there is one final thing I want to refer you to in this document. The very last page of the document, section J. And that is the section stating: "Demarche by Head of Mission on behalf of the CMS," that's the council, "of 4 October with Karadzic and Boban." Could you perhaps just give the Court an idea of what this demarche was about?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: This was a rare thing but a demarche was issued by the European Union and it was to try and directly address the issue of blocking of humanitarian aid, and it was something which I believe was addressed at all of the warring factions and here we see the contents specifically mentioning that we should have freedom of movement for humanitarian aid.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, sir, stepping off this document, after the meeting with Jadranko Prlic, is it correct that you then went for lunch with him?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: Yes. He invited the ambassador, Sir Martin Garrod, the head of the regional centre, and myself to lunch, and he was accompanied by Slobodan Bozic, the deputy minister of defence, and also responsible, I believe, for relations with the international community.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Could you tell the Court what happened during this luncheon?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: Yes. Actually it hadn't been part of the planned itinerary and we arrived at Mr. Prlic's office and he very kindly offered to take us out to lunch and it was quite difficult to say no.
