So we went, but we did state very clearly that there was further elements of the programme including a visit to East Mostar that we felt was important to achieve, and therefore the lunch may have to be concluded early, and indeed it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Could you tell the Court about the exchange that took place when you indicated that you were going to leave this lunch earlier?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: Yes. I think it was obviously quite awkward having been invited to -- to break that lunch, but I was insistent knowing that we had to meet the Muslim leadership, and this caused a little bit of consternation and a little exchange between Mr. Prlic and Mr. Bozic. Mr. Bozic then left and later made a call, I believe, returned and said that it was all sorted for our passage. The next day I met Slobodan Bozic, and he was concerned and annoyed and was -- said that we should give warning when we were travelling to East Mostar to ensure there were no incidents, and indeed we had an incident-free visit later on that afternoon immediately after the lunch.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Did you have any idea or could you form any idea of how it came that there were no incidents when you visited West Mostar that day?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to object. My learned friend knows better than that. That's really calling for speculation. I think the fact that there were no incidents speaks for itself, but now to ask the gentleman to speculate, I think it goes beyond the pale. Unless the gentleman can tell us concretely if he knows anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: I think if we allow the witness to answer then it would become clear, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could you pose the question again? Sorry, I need to --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, you said there was an incident-free visit to Mostar when you left the luncheon with Mr. Prlic, and the question was, did you have any idea, were you able to form any idea of how it came that this was incident free?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: Well, not every time we went to East Mostar were there incidents, but clearly our statement that we were going and we were going that afternoon caused consternation. A communication was made. We didn't have any incidents. There may have or may not have been instructions given. I can only say that we didn't have a -- any incidents that afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, the word "incident" has been used here in English. Line 14, page 46, "incidents" in the plural form. What is, in your view, an incident in East Mostar? What could have happened there if there had been incidents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A range of possibilities. First, we may not have been physically able to get there. Perhaps our passage and freedom of movement would have been prevented. That didn't happen. There were no direct or aggressive acts against us as individuals or our vehicles, which sometimes happened. We were sometimes sniped at. We had armoured vehicles. It wasn't uncommon that those armoured vehicles received small-arms attraction. There were no detonations of mortar or artillery or tank rounds in East Mostar during the period of that visit. So it was a smooth passage in terms of movement and no aggression against us and no observed or heard detonations or explosions during that particular period. So that's what I meant, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Witness, if we may turn to a different document, and this is Exhibit 6381. Exhibit 6381. And this is a special report dated the 8th of November, 1993, and we read right at the beginning: "Please find hereunder an incident report by Philip Watkins, HCC Travnik." Looking at this report, is this indeed a report drafted by you?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: It has -- first of all, I supplied a report but I did so in my report as HCC Mostar, and I see that's been annotated here. So Travnik was wrong. It was actually issued by the political section by the headquarters in Zagreb, but it would have been based, as stated here, on a special report that I wrote and passed up through the headquarters of Zenica and from Zenica on to Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: So based on what you say, looking from the introduction further in the various sections, would that have been the contents of your original report?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, if we look at the introduction, paragraph 2, and it deals here with the origins of the republic. "The origins -- the origins of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna lies in the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna or can be found in the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. The CCHB was established to promote the interests of Croats within Bosnia-Herzegovina. Many of the senior politicians now in the CRHB held positions in this organisation." Could you comment on this?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: Yes. This was the maturing of the self-styled Croatian republic, and certain members, including Mr. Prlic, who had been the president of the government of the CCHB, was now emerging as the president of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: The next part says: "The other source of political experience in the Croatian republic are those who held positions in the Bosnian-Herzegovinian government. They have -- the latter have abandoned the BiH parliament stating that it is unconstitutional having been hijacked by the Muslims." Could you comment on this one?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: Yeah, the C -- the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna was, if you like, gathering political experience, and some of that political experience had been evident by individuals playing a role in the internationally recognised Republic of Bosnia-Hercegovina over time and during the fighting, and because of the fighting and many other reasons, there was an increasing view articulated by the Bosnian Croats that the legitimacy of the Sarajevo government had been eroded, that while recognised by the international community it didn't have the legitimacy it once had because, for instance, the Bosnian Serbs had left the government and the Croatian republic was a better manifestation of the interests of the Bosnian Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, sir, in the set-up of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, were you aware of any elections that took place?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: No. And as noted here, the -- it would have been impossible to have held any meaningful elections, but there was a genuine attempt to demonstrate legitimacy by noting that many of these key post holders that were emerging either in the government or in the Presidency or indeed as members of parliament had once been elected when the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina was formed. So there was a legitimacy, an audit trail of legitimacy, if you like, back to, for instance, municipality elections that had taken place of elected mayors and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: If we turn the page to paragraph 5, Government. And here we have a statement of: "Ministers have not been elected. They have been temporarily employed in caretaker positions or roles. And then the president of the government will present its nominations to the House of Representatives for the ratification on 10 November 1993." Could you comment on that, explain that?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: Yes, this is this period of sort of fluidity of uncertainty as to exactly who was filling what role and what the functions of the various elements of government were going to be, and so there was a government that was being put together and it was being put together by Mr. Prlic and there would be temporary announcements, and indeed you can see in the paragraph below some of the known ones were -- were, I have filled in, but it was made clear to me that these would need a ratification and that that ratification was to come at a later stage. Well, it says here 10th of November.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: The question marks against some of the names under the 13 ministries, what do those question marks signify?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: It simply means that at the moment that I wrote this report I could not put a particular name. I think quite soon after and rapidly over the coming weeks we were able to fill in most of those blanks but at this time it's because I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, if we look at the first paragraph of this section, it says the known positions in the government which are considered secure are as follows, and then it lists president of the government, Prlic, and then under that Valenta. Could you comment on what basis they were seen as being secure in their positions?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: Well, by having meetings with as many individuals in key positions as I could, one began to sort of triangulate and cross-check information, and I don't think there was any doubt that Mr. Prlic was going to be the president of the government. There was, however, considerable uncertainty about the roles of some of the central -- central Bosnian -- the Bosnian Croats in Central Bosnia. By that I mean Kordic and Valenta in particular, but also some others from Zepce and Zavidovici, Mr. Lozancic, and one or two others. The names will probably spring to me in a moment, and we were very interested to know what role those leading players in Central Bosnia were going to play in this newly formed administration. So Mr. Prlic secured Valenta. By that time I'd obviously got enough information for me to be confident, but I do remember that was one position we were uncertain of.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, Anto Valenta, did you ever meet Anto Valenta?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: Yes, I met Anto Valenta in Central Bosnia in Vitez when I was the head of CC Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: We'll come back to the in due course. Sir, against the Ministry of Defence is the name of Branko Stojic. Could that be a mistake and could that perhaps be Bruno Stojic?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: Yes, it is Bruno Stojic. There is no doubt in my mind that he had been the Minister of Defence under the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna and there was no suggestion at this stage that he wasn't going to continue that role, although he was later replaced by Perica Jukic as the minister of defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, could --

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: Perica Jukic would be a good example of someone out of Herzegovina up in Central Bosnia. I think his hometown was either Zepce -- it was Zepce or Zavidovici. That was his political power base, I think, as the mayor of Zepce, and we were interested in how they would be drawn into this government.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: If I can refer you finally on this document to -- no -- penultimately, paragraph 6, house of representatives, and could you perhaps just explain what -- what this is about, the 70 members of the house of representatives?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: Well, the house of representatives was going to be the sort of members of parliament, and from the members of parliament Mr. Prlic was going to select his government, and the members of parliament would then ratify that government. So the 70 members, I think this was -- this was a figure that was yet settled, but, but it was going to certainly as trying to send a signal of legitimacy include, and I note here 21 of the presidents of the municipality, i.e., mayors who had been elected under the elections that took place to form the structures of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, these 13 ministers, did I understand correctly that they would have been appointed from within the house of representatives?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: I -- yes, that was my understanding yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: If we can turn the page to other, the last page of the document. Paragraph 7. So it says, other recently formed Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna instruments, and it says, "Vladislav Pogarcic informs that they are presidential appointments of Mate Boban, and the officers and institutions have authority for the following," and then the list of -- of officers or institutions follow. Could you comment on -- on this?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: Yes. This was of considerable interest to us that Mate Boban appeared to be forming a group of advisors, a series of offices which he seemed to be controlling, and we didn't understand what the relationship of that office would be to the government. Would they receive legitimacy through the government? Would the government ultimately control them? It appeared that there were almost two structures forming, one around Mate Boban and then the government and the house of representatives. And we were later able to put some names next to the -- to these offices. And I remember Mr. Pogarcic himself was to become the advisor on human rights and some element of international relations, and I believe that Mr. Pusic was to be head of the office of refugees and displaced persons, but I may be -- stand corrected there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: That is under item C.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: Yes. It may have changed its name, but at a later stage we were able to verify that Mr. Pusic seemed to have a direct link with Mr. Boban through this structure we were slightly unsure of its constitutional role or these offices and their constitutional role.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you. If we can step on to another document, Exhibit 6 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me. Mr. Kruger, I'm terribly sorry to interrupt, but I have to interrupt at this point. The paragraph number 7, sir, as we read it, it seemed, and I do say that it would seem that at the reading of this paragraph we can conclude that Mr. Mate Boban appointed the officials of various offices that are enumerated here, and we can count six offices exactly. One of them is the office of refugees and displaced persons. You've stated earlier that were two parallel structures. One which is a governmental structure presided by Mr. Prlic, and another structure presided by Boban with these offices. When you drafted this paragraph, paragraph number 7, what source did you use? Who informed you of this, and how were you able to confirm this or to assert this? Is this an assertion that was not yet an assertion? Was it a certainty, or was it something that was supposed to happen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sir, when I said parallel structures, I think what was being presented to us was a coherent state with a Presidency, a government, and House of Representatives. Our interest was understanding where the power lay within that, and it wasn't clear whether that was one coherent state or whether there were going to be power struggles. When I wrote this report, the source of information about the four offices and two institutions was Vladislav Pogarcic, and clearly at the moment that I wrote this report I was not able to put names next to it. So he was telling me of an intent. I think that if I'd had the names at that stage I would have put them because I was keen to do so on the previous page when I did have names. So it was a forge self-styled republic about which we were gathering information, and at the time of this report I could not put names next to those offices, and the source of information about those offices was primarily Mr. Pogarcic, but also, sir, I remember another media advisor whose name was Lozancic, and there was another media advisor called Maric, and these were people that we talked to, to try and get as much information as we could, but primarily, sir, to be clear it was Pogarcic who informed me of the structures forming around Mate Boban.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: If we may turn to document 6473. And this is an ECMM CC Mostar daily summary for 6 November 1993. Do you have the document?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Is this a report by you?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, sir, if we look under paragraph 1. This just builds on the previous document we saw. Actually, it precedes it. In the very first section, Political, about two-thirds of the way through that first paragraph it says: "Jadranko Prlic, president of the government of CRHB had been authorised by parliament to form a government. Prlic would make his recommendations and these would then be ratified or not." And do you have any further comments on that?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: This is a good example of how we tried to gather information, and I used the term before, triangulate. So we went to see the president of Grude, the mayor of Grude, and his assertion corresponded what we heard before that Mr. Prlic would make a recommendation and these would be ratified. The comment that I make here, "it seems that parliament will ratify rather than elect," is again confirmation that elections in these circumstances were external to give validity to the Presidency were unlikely. What wasn't clear was whether there would actually be a vote within the Presidency, which would of course have been possible but here it seems to suggest a ratification, a rubber-stamping rather than a real democratic nomination and legitimacy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you. If you turn the page to paragraph 7, Assessment. And your assessment which you give here is the statement by Jozo Maric demonstrates Jadranko Prlic is safely established as president of the government of CRHB. The future for others may not be so secure. Do you want to comment on that further?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: Yes. This is beginning of November, and as I think I said before, it have the end of December before we had full ratification. So I'm sending an early signal that I'm getting enough information from different sources to suggest that Mr. Prlic -- there is no threat to his personal position as a transfer of president of the CCHB to the president of the CRHB. "The future of others may not be so secure," well, again this is reference to what I said earlier about who else would or would not survive the transition from a community of interests to a self-styled republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Okay. Is sir, one further aspect on this document. If you turn to the first page again and look at Military. Jozo Maric then also is reported as giving some views on the Stupni Do massacre, and he revealed that "outside elements had participated the attack," and then it goes further. Could you comment on this explanation given by him?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: Just to be clear, this is where it says, "this condemned the Muslim occupation of Muslim territory in Central Bosnia and condemned the synchronised attack on Vares." I don't see the specific reference to Stupni Do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sorry, if you look under Military?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: Oh, under there. Yeah, got it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: First paragraph under Military.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: Yeah. This was -- 6th of November would have been about two -- two weeks after Stupni Do, and I think I said earlier there were very different and confusing versions of what had happened but here we see an example, I think an early recognition which we have already stated, Mr. Prlic agreeing what had happened and here is another person saying that, "outside elements." Well, outside elements could have referred to -- to Mujahedin, for instance. I wanted clarification. Did he mean Muslim or Croat elements? And he says -- or I report that he says, "Maric answered that rogue HVO from Kakanj and Kiseljak seemed to be involved." Well, that very much corresponded with our own information that the Stupni Do massacre was committed by HVO elements commanded by Ivica Rajic who was the brigade commander in Kiseljak-Busovaca -- Kiseljak area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Just two lines further there's this following sentence: "The massacre was the excuse the armija wanted and the coordinated attack by the 2nd and 3rd Corps of Vares proved they were prepared." Can you comment on this? What was meant by this?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: The Vares pocket was vulnerable militarily. There had been much speculation that the armija forces from 2nd Corps and 3rd Corps, 2nd Corps being Tuzla based and 3rd Corps being Zenica based would try and retake that territory, and they would need justification for that otherwise there would be international condemnation because there would undoubtedly have been significant humanitarian issues resulting with the movement of that population, the Bosnian Croat population out of Vares. So that's -- that's what this refers to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you. If we can step on to the next document, is document -- or Exhibit 6382. Document -- or Exhibit 6382. This is an ECMM daily summary report from CC Mostar dated the 3rd of November. Do you have the document?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: Yes. It's one I wrote.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, sir, I see that there are certain annotations or markings on this. Can you perhaps just cast some light on that?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: I can only say they weren't put on by me because this would have been electronically transmitted, and it was a recipient somewhere that put that cross and those two lines, but not me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if we look at the first page, Political, the first paragraph, "HCC and M2 and 3 met Ivan Bender." HCC, that was you?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: That's me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Mm-hmm. And the last sentence then in the paragraph, it says that the current appointments were caretaker with the exception of Mate Boban, and this appears to be Ivan Bender. Can you comment on this?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: Yes another example of a political lead are trying to get another angle, perhaps a little bit more information on who was in what position and it seemed -- this was written on the 3rd of November so really quite early on, even though it -- in the last document. Yeah. The issue of Mate Boban and his position was really -- by this time we were getting lots of rumours, and he's saying that Mate Boban's position is firm. "The rest," he said, "are caretaker," and I note that he's -- puts down the president of the government there as a caretaker.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now immediately after the names, can you comment on that sentence, "When parliament has elected the government position of president of the government. Will assume primacy, but until then Perica Jukic was senior to Jadranko Prlic." Could you comment on that?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: The role of Perica Jukic was -- I think he was president of the house of representatives, and also by this time beginning to be mentioned as a possible minister of defence, and I think we were unsure as to which position he would hold. And here we're getting a very clear steer from Mr. Bender that actually Mr. Jukic has the upper hand at the moment, because until Mr. Prlic -- "the upper hand," by that I mean the senior position, that Mr. Prlic is awaiting some sort of endorsement, some sort of constitutional endorsement. What later happened was -- well, Jadranko Prlic retained his primacy. I don't believe it was ever seriously threatened, but there were some interesting manoeuvres going on there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, if we can step on to another document, Exhibit 6687. Exhibit 6687. And that is daily is summary or summary report from CC Mostar dated 16 November 1993. Do you have the document?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: It's a document that I wrote.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, if we can look under point 1, Political, the very first paragraph. It reports a meeting -- or you report a meeting with Slobodan Lovrenovic.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Could you perhaps just tell us who he was?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: Yes. This is the person I was referring to, or one of the people I was referring to earlier. He was a press advisor to Mate Boban and quite a good source of information.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, he mentions, "Lovrenovic said the House of Representatives will convene on 20 November 1993. They will provide legal confirmation of Jadranko Prlic for nomination of ministers." Can you comment on that? Was this a postponement or had this already been scheduled prior to this -- to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: Yeah, we had the statement earlier on, that it was scheduled. I think it was the 10th of November, so it hadn't happened now and we were interested in when it would happen, and we're told in four days' time, 20th of November.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Looking at the next part -- sentence, Lovrenovic was asked whether Prlic or Boban has primacy in selection of Obrenovic in selection of ministers and replied, "Prlic himself had stated it was essentially his choice but with the president's input." Could you comment on this, please?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: Yes and a good example of where we're trying to understand the relationship between Prlic and Boban, who has primacy is -- is the choice really with Prlic or is Boban -- does Boban have the final say? And it's being suggested to -- to us here that it is Mr. Prlic's choice, but not detracting from the fact that Mr. Boban would have an input into who that would be. So my understanding was there was going to be collaboration between the two, that Mr. Prlic would not independently be able to put those forward without some sort of endorsement from Mate Boban.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, now, at the bottom of that page the next section starts, Military. If we then turn to the next page. And if we look at the very first paragraph on that page. It says Lieutenant General Ante Roso has replaced General Praljak as commander. This is in line with your recollection and what you testified earlier.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: Yes, it is. A succession of the Supreme Commander of HVO. We knew and I think that earlier statement showed we were trying to reach General Praljak. He wasn't around, and then it becomes clear that there is a new senior commander emerging, and it's lieutenant General Ante Roso.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: If we can just take note of the following part where he says that Praljak -- he said that, "Praljak had been honourably retired due to mental fatigue. There was to question of him having been dismissed." Just take note of that, and we will come back to this topic a bit later on. I just highlight it at this stage. The next paragraph, I'd like your comments on Jadranko Prlic met Ante Roso to introduce measures introduced to ensure the observance of codes of war. And then, "a brochure has been issued to all HVO units detailing regulations regarding treatment of POWs," et cetera, et cetera. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: I do see that. What I can't comment on unless it's somewhere else and I read the whole -- this report is -- what the source of that information or where it came from, but what I am reporting here is something of interest because we have the political situation emerging and we have a new military leader, and of course we're interested in -- in the relationship between the military and the political leadership and it appears here that we have the new commander talking with the president of the government trying to ensure new observance of codes of war, again providing more surety and more legitimacy to the self-styled republic that was forming.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Could you comment from your experience as the head of CC Mostar at that stage on the involvement of Jadranko Prlic in this aspect?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: Sorry, in what particular aspect? It was clear --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sorry, on the -- on -- ensuring the compliance with the code of war and the issuance of this brochure, talking to Roso.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: Well, I think if you're establishing a new republic what's important would be important to the international community is that in fact the political leadership has command over the military forces, and it appears that we have a meeting of the two key leaders of -- or a key leader in the political structure with a key leader of the military structure to do what's stated there, to -- to suggest -- it suggests that up until now there may well have been, and indeed I believe there were, Codes of Conduct, but here is a new moment to ensure either that those that are there are implemented or that new codes are formed. A demonstration of a legal structure connecting political with military right down to the troops on the front line understanding a command structure and a conduct of war, what's acceptable and what isn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Okay. To your understanding, or do you have any idea or could you shed light on the position that Jadranko Prlic occupied in the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna as opposed to what he had previously been in, in the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: Well, it was essentially the same thing Prime Minister of the Croatian Community and Prime Minister of the republic, but I think we're seeing the formation of something which was more defined, more legally secure, more credible as an interface with other republics, such as the Bosnian Serb Republic, and also trying to establish a legitimacy in the international community's eyes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, if I may refer you to the final section of this document. Paragraph 7, Assessment. And here you say the information provided by Lovrenovic has to be confirmed, but the statement that "Kordic and Valenta do not hold executive office is significant." Could you comment on that and why it would be significant?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: Yes. This is -- this is again referring to what is the role of the central Bosnian Croat leadership, and there was endless speculation and end the different interpretations, because while I was meeting the senior leaders in -- in Mostar, of course, the teams up in -- teams up in Central Bosnia were talking to Mr. Kordic, Mr. Valenta, and there were different stories coming out as to what roles they were going to play. And it appears here from Mr. Lovrenovic that Kordic and Valenta are not going to hold executive office is of great interest to us. Well, if they're not, why not, and that's contrary to reports we're getting elsewhere. So we need to get, well, more information and keep sort of pushing and pressing on this to find out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: You mention in this paragraph a political divide between the Croats of Central Bosnia and those of Herzegovina as the subject of debate. Would you like to elaborate any further on the divide you refer to?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: The -- broadly speaking, and this is a bit of a generalisation, I think the further you moved away from Mostar and up into Central Bosnia and up into Tuzla, then you perhaps found less certainty in some of the understanding as to what the future of -- of the Croats would be. You were vulnerable if you were a Bosnian Croat in Central Bosnia or up in -- in the Tuzla area, and you perhaps could not afford to take positions which were as stark and voiced as clearly as those in Mostar. They had a certainty about creating a republic that had a concentration of the Croatian Community which will territorial integrity, and I think you felt vulnerable and there were lots of discussions about, well, if we were moving towards an internationally acceptable, three-republic solution to Bosnia-Herzegovina, there would have to be boundaries drawn, and if you were in Herzegovina, it was very clear that you were going to be in the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna. If you lived in Tuzla or Vares or Zepce or Zavidovici, you probably weren't quite so certain, and so there were differences being articulated by leaders, depending where you were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you. How many times in all would you say you met Jadranko Prlic? If you could give the Court an estimate.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: I would say somewhere between, I don't know, eight and -- 8, 10, 12 times. Probably nearer -- yeah, 8 to 10, I'd say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: This was as head of CC Mostar?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: No. I would say that was more than that, because of course I -- I also dealt with Mr. Prlic at a later stage when I became the head of the regional centre in BiH. I would say during this period I probably -- which is October to January, a four-month period. I probably saw him six to eight sometimes, something in that -- that -- certainly more than -- not every week, but every -- every couple of weeks, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: When you dealt with him later as -- was that as head of RC Zenica?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: It was, although RC Zenica then changed its name to RC BiH.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Mm-hmm. What was his capacity at that stage?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: The Federation had been formed, and he was still a senior member of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, but I think by then he had become the Foreign Minister of the Federation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: After this and after having left the ECMM, could you tell the Court briefly of any other dealings you had with Mr. Prlic?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: Yes. I left ECMM in 1995 and then the UN for a short period, and then I then set up this business, and the business was involved in trying to get companies involved in reconstruction, to take advantage of the 5.2 billion dollar restoration package. And I felt I was quite well placed. I'd made many contacts at senior leadership level, and companies that wanted to get involved were interested in the opportunities but concerned about the situation and no knowledge. So I created a company with some colleagues, a consultancy that was going to try and facilitate entry of companies, and to that effect I made contact with many of the people I previously dealt with in ECMM, and Mr. Prlic was one of those.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, sir, you -- we touched upon Ante Valenta earlier, and you said you had met him. Can you tell the Court approximately when it was you met him?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: That would have been in my position of HCC Travnik, so it would have been between June and October. I don't remember exactly but certainly July, August, September.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Where did you meet him?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: I met him in the headquarters of operational zone middle Bosna in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Could you tell the Court about the -- the meeting you had with him what you discussed?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: Well I met him several times but on one particular occasion I was -- I had a meeting with him and the discussion was about the future of Bosnia, and Mr. Valenta treated me to one of his explorations of movements of population which he felt -- which he demonstrated happened, I think, historically, but how he saw the future moments of population to secure very clearly boundaries and divisions between the two ethnic groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Did he show you any documents or --

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: Yes. He referred to a book that he'd written and -- and I was shown that, but not a translation of it. And he showed me some maps, maps with arrows demonstrating movements of population. Some were looking at a -- a Bosnia-Herzegovina level with large movements, sort of hundred thousand this way and a hundred thousand that way, but also some more fine-grained maps of what was -- what should happen in Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: If you say referring hundred thousand in this way and hundred thousand in that way, could you perhaps be more specific?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: Yes. I'm not sure it was a hundred thousand; it was large numbers. But he was suggesting that the future of Bosnia-Herzegovina lay not in an integrated, mixed community but in the separation and establishment of three political states, and that the way that would provide there would be security in the future in a way that hadn't happened in the past was to ensure that they were largely ethnically pure and concentrated. So he saw movements would be required in any settlement of Bosnian Croats into Bosnian Croat-held territory primarily in Herzegovina, and in fact extending into Central Bosnia. He saw the movement of Muslims out of Croat and Serb areas and concentrating in an area, Sarajevo-Sandzak, and he saw other movements of Croats out of Bosnian Serb territory and vice versa. Big movements of the three populations to establish ethnically pure, or nearer than they were at the moment, states.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, if I can refer you to Exhibit 21. Exhibit 00021. It's the very first one in the binder you have. And if you can ignore the translation at the beginning and move directly at -- to the B/C/S or the original version.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: I have that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, sir, is it correct that you had an opportunity during our meeting prior to your testimony to have a look at this document and page through it?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And what is this document?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: I believe this document is the -- is a translation of that book which I referred to a moment ago, Mr. Valenta's Vision of the Future.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: If you can go beyond the translation to the original document --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may lodge an objection or an observation at this point in time. While I have no -- no problem with the gentleman going through the document itself, first I would like a foundation, whether the gentleman was provided with a full translation of the book at that time when he met Mr. Valenta. That's number one. Next two, if he was not, is this the first time he's looking at the excerpts that were provided by the Prosecution? If the answer is yes to the latter, then I would object to the gentleman commenting about the books obviously he told us what he was told by Mr. Valenta. To now comment on excerpts of the book without giving the gentleman the opportunity to read the entire book, I think, would be a disservice to the testimony, because I think we need to put it into context. So perhaps we could have a foundation and then we'll see how I'll -- whether I will object or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. If I may just respond to that and then hopefully set the mind of my learned colleague at rest. The Prosecution does not intend to go into the book in any depth. The purpose of showing this is merely to ascertain whether this is indeed the book he refers to when he says that a book was shown to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, then, Your Honour, and again I don't mean to be disputatious, but if the gentleman could be shown whatever was shown to him. So if a Bosnian version was shown to him or a Croatian version, they could show him, but to show them excerpts of a translated version and say, "Was this shown to you?", unless the gentleman -- unless you can establish that the gentleman reads and understands B/C/S, I don't see how he can simply answer the question at this point in time. Again, I have no objection to the entire book coming into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kruger, please put your question to the witness, because if you're dealing with Exhibit 21, you certainly have a reason. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, you mentioned the -- the fact that Mr. Valenta also showed you maps. I would like to refer you to page 43 of the B/C/S version. And my simple question to you is: Just looking at that map as it is there, do you recall maps such as this being shown to you and being discussed with Mr. Valenta?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: Yes. This is the -- the type of map that I was shown.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: If you can look at page 66. The map on page 66, do you recall this map specifically?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: This is consistent with the mapping that I was shown on that day, the large arrows with big movements indicated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, if we can step off that document. Just one further question on Mr. Valenta and his views as he explained them to you as well. Did you hear his views being discussed in any other forum during your period as an ECMM monitor?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: He made the same presentation to Jean-Pierre Thebault, the head of mission, and I believe that most internationals who visited him were given the opportunity to listen to his views. There was an interesting dynamic within the -- within Vitez. I do remember that before I saw Mr. Valenta I actually met Tihomir Blaskic, a commander of the operative zone middle Bosna, and said I was going to see Mr. Valenta, and there was a certain nod and a certain smile, and certainly the liaison officers sort of said -- well, good luck was the indication they were giving. There was some lack of respect given to the ideas that were coming out by those immediately sharing the same building space.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, sir, turning to Bruno Stojic for a moment, we've already discussed your -- the fact that you didn't actually have direct dealings with him. If I may refer you to Exhibit 04083. So 4083. And this is a ECMM daily summary or summary report dated 10 August 1993, from team V2 HBC Travnik to RC Zenica. My first question is do you recall this report or can you comment on whether you would know it?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: This is actually a report from the head -- the HCC Travnik, so it's -- it's a report from me to Regional Centre Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you. And if I may refer you to point 1 and under point 2 political activity and if you turn to the second paragraph and this it relates what happened during a meeting with Pero Skopljak. He indicated that Mr. Boban and the military did not enjoy mutual confidence, and it goes on. A little further down it says that, "There's talk of an alleged Stojic-Boban rift which could suggest that the leadership is suffering under the strain of HVO defeats." Could you comment on this?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: Well, I guess this is the beginning of those issues to which I earlier referred of Boban's position. I didn't know Mr. Stojic then except by -- by name and appointment, and it's obviously suggesting here that there is a rift, but the other interesting point is suffering under the strain of -- of HVO defeats. The military situation in Central Bosnia on 10th of August wasn't good. There had been the fighting in Busovaca in the Vrbas and Lasva Valley in January tempered for a few months by these joint commissions that were set up in both areas. Then we have the breakout of fighting between the Croats and Muslims in April time, and, if you like, at a tactical level the winners in Central Bosnia were the armija forces. The HVO had not achieved their military successes, and I think the feeling in Central Bosnia was that there had been an expectation from Mostar that the HVO forces would have achieved more than they had. They had failed to gain territory. Indeed, they had lost territory, and that there was a political impact on Mr. Boban as a result of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, if we can turn to General Praljak and focus on him for a while. When was the first time that you met General Praljak?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: I met him when I was head of CC Travnik, and I met him actually by chance when I visited the Rama Brigade headquarters and the operational zone headquarters in Prozor and discovered General Praljak there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And could you give an indication on approximately when this was?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: It would have been round about August, possibly July 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: How did you find General Praljak as a person at that time?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: He was very open, very engaging. He received us well. We had -- he answered the questions directly and in fact was a contrast to often what you found with the military leadership, which was a tendency not to want to give information. Quite the opposite in General Praljak. He was quite expansive about his role and his views and some wider issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Did he indicate anything about his -- his own background?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: Yes. He told me that he had served in the HV in Vukovar. He told me that he's -- he'd also been involved in the theatre I believe in some capacity, director or producer, and also that he had a background in psychology.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Did you talk to General Praljak about his status at that time?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: Yes. He told me that he was in command and General Petkovic wasn't. Now, this is the first time that I'd met General Praljak, and I don't actually think that many, if any, other members of the international community had either. So I was very interested in who was commander, was it Petkovic or was it General Praljak, and he made it very clear that he was in command and that General Petkovic reported to him, and I think he actually described him as the Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Was there any talk about the relationship between General Petkovic and Mate Boban that you can recall?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: Not immediately, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, did you speak to General Praljak about humanitarian aid?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: Yes. I took the opportunity to address a range of issues, freedom of movement being one of those, freedom of movement for ECMM, freedom of movement for UN, and in particular freedom of movement for UNHCR convoys. And General Praljak was very clear that there needed to be a military solution to the situation and whatever means were necessary should be taken, and he actually said to me that that would include the stopping of convoys, and it would include the cutting off of water.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Stopping of convoys going where and cutting off of water to whom?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: Well, supplies of utilities, be it water or electricity, were obviously very contentious issues, particularly as lines and sources of those utilities were inevitably held by different groups. So they were always being played off. The water source for Zenica was held in Kruscica, and you'd find the people of Kruscica turning off the water that not only supplied Zenica, but it also supplied the Croats. So it was forever being used as tool. The supply of humanitarian aid was always an issue because while I was recognised that isolated pockets needed humanitarian aid, there was also the concern often articulated that humanitarian aid was merely sustaining military units as well as a civilian population. And what General Praljak was saying to me was all means should be brought to bear to defeat the armija, and that would include stopping what he saw as the supply of -- of food, and he also mentioned, as I say, the water.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Okay. Did you and General Praljak discuss anything concerning the army of the Republic of Croatia and their -- their soldiers?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: Yes. I think within a matter of days of arrival in Bosnia it became very clear to me that a consistent concern coming through was the involvement of outside elements. As I said before, that could be Mujahedin in this case and regularly there were reports of HV involvement, Croatian republic troops involved in Bosnia. And we took every opportunity we could to -- to find out more. And General Praljak said to me very clearly that the HV were not involved in Bosnia. When I referred to individual soldiers who you sometimes saw wearing HV insignia, he explained that, like himself, they were born in Bosnia. They may have served in the Croatian army, and they were returning as individuals to support the Bosnian Croats and their families. That was his explanation. Individuals and not units.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: The presence of the -- of HV components in Bosnia at that stage, was there something which interested the ECMM?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: We had reports, as I say, from many sources, and primarily it was from the armija, the armija saying that various units were in certain locations. And we often investigated that, but we were never able to get anything definitive until, in my own personal circumstances, January 1994, possibly early February, I forget the exact date, when I was returning to Herzegovina from a meeting in Central Bosnia, and I was returning with the head of the regional centre, Martin Garrod, and we were travelling on the main routes, Diamond and Triangle, and bad conditions. We had to pull over to allow a military convoy to pass us travelling up towards Prozor. That was the first time I saw definitively a formed military unit where there was almost no pretense to hide what it was. It was an HV unit, and I made a report of what we saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Okay. We'll get to that at a later stage. So if I could just perhaps then go back to the original question. The presence of HVO components in Bosnia or not, was this something that -- that was being actively monitored or looked at by the ECMM?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: Can I just confirm you mean HV?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: HV. My apologies. Was the presence of HV something which interested the ECMM?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: Yes, it did. Not just ECMM. The United Nations, the international community, because it would send signals of the involvement in another state -- internationally recognised military forces in a -- internationally recognised state of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: In your meeting with Mr. Praljak was HVO strategy in Central Bosnia a topic of discussion there or goals?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: Yes. There had been much speculation that the HVO were going to carry out an offensive pushing from the Prozor front line either down towards Gornji Vakuf to secure routes in or actually alternatively straight across through -- through, up to the so-called Kakanj area. This was, in my estimation and many others, very unlikely. The HVO had not proved themselves capable of making that sort of military gain. Indeed, where there had been attempts to made military gain it -- in Central Bosnia, it had been set back. So it was going to need a different dynamic to alter that balance of forces. That's why the HV and the HV's involvement was so important. But in discussions about the future, and this is at the time when we're still -- international community is looking and exploring the idea of a three -- three-republic solution to Bosnia-Herzegovina, along with the issues of Mr. Valenta and movements of population were, well, if you're going to form that republic it has to have a border and boundary, and where is that going to be? Would it be at the front line as it existed in Prozor or was it more ambitious? Did it include Central Bosnia and? And General Praljak said to me very clearly that there was no way that they were going to accept a Croatian republic that didn't include Vitez and the Lasva Valley as part of Herzegovina. However, and he specifically mentioned that Tuzla and Vares may be -- as part of the deal, they could be conceded to one of the other republics.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Did you take stage talk to General Praljak about access to Muslim families in Prozor?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: Yeah. We -- as part of our role in ECMM, as I said earlier, I was trying to visit isolated communities be that Bosnian Croat in Central Bosnia or -- or Muslim communities, and because I had been involved specifically with Prozor since the very first day, I had been in -- in Bosnia, the issue of the situation for the Muslims in Prozor was of interest to me, and we had regularly tried to and sometimes had achieved gaining access to the imam of Prozor as a signal, if you like, that we -- we knew of their position, their existence, their predicament, and we had found it difficult, and I believe one of my teams had been prevented from seeing the imam. So I asked General Praljak directly about this and he said he would guarantee me access to prisoners of war and to the imam.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And did that happen?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: My recollection is that we did gain access to the imam, again, after that discussion. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And to prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: Ah. Prisoners of war was more contentious. Access to alleged detention camps and prisoner of war camps was something which ECMM was interested in. It was primarily the responsibility to negotiate terms of prisoners and access -- that of the International Committee of the Red Cross, the ICRC; however, we took a keen interest in this and there was rarely access granted by either the Bosnian Muslims and the armija forces to HVO-held prisoners or access to Bosnian Croats. We did achieve it sometimes. I personally achieved it at Gromiljak where I saw -- I went to a camp, and I actually instigated that all my teams when I became HCC Mostar should try and gain access to certain camps, and again with very little success but with a little bit of success.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: After this first meeting did you meet with General Praljak again?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I met him once more for -- did I remember on the Makljen ridge, which is the front line just north of Prozor where I actually met him in the field. I have tried very hard to recollect why I was on the Makljen ridge but -- and why I went to this particular area, but -- broadly it was because of this belief that there were forces gathering to -- to go on the offensive. And I met him with a UN observer whose surname I forgot, but I do remember his first name was Randy and he was a US citizen, and we had a discussion. I don't honestly remember the detail of that discussion but, again, very open. Never doing anything other than engaging me in conversation and not hiding his answers. He was very open in his answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, do we have -- do we have time for one more document, or shall we break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One more document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: If we may look very quickly at document 6244. 06244. And this is an ECMM CC Mostar daily summary for 29 October 1993. Is this a report by you?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: It doesn't have my signature, but I do believe it is a report by me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, if I can very quickly refer you section 5 on the first page. Humanitarian. And very last paragraph on that page. A meeting between HVO General Praljak and BiH was schedule for today. The meeting was initiated by the HVO but was cancelled because Pasalic refused to attend. Could you recall this?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: I'm sorry I have inadvertently turned to 6424, and I see on the screen 6244 is the one you want me to actually look at.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: 6244. My apologies?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: In this case it is signed by me. It is my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you. The section humanitarian?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And the very last paragraph at the bottom of that page. "A meeting between Praljak and BiH was scheduled but was cancelled because Pasalic refused to attend."

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: Yes. Well, obviously at this stage, 29th of October, we very much believe that it's General Praljak we need to see to get a resolution to the helicopter issue. Interesting to note that it appears the HVO were willing to have this meeting, but in this case General Pasalic wasn't, and I guess it's an indication of how important in terms of negotiations and positions hostage -- prisoner of war exchange was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Okay. Under Political, the first paragraph M3 had a meeting with Mr. Markovic and then this meeting is reported. Do you know who Mr. Markovic was?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: Yes. And it states he was the mayor of Stolac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Mm-hmm. Did you ever meet with him?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: His first name, Pero Markovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Mm-hmm?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: Yes, I believe I did, but not on this occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. It's 20 to 6.00. We will have a 20-minute break and resume at 6.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The hearing is resumed. First Mr. Registrar for a list, an IC numbers.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours. The Prosecution response to the exhibits tendered through Witness BC by the Accused Jadranko Prlic, Defence team number 1, will become Exhibit number IC 575 under seal. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. You have the floor again, Mr. Kruger.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, if we may go to Exhibit 6731. Yes, I see you want to --

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: Yes. This is -- this is slightly out of context, but just before we start the new session I have remembered the name of the Swedish monitor. It was Mr. Junhov, who I took over from when I took over as HCC Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: J-u-n-h-o-v.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: That doings remind me, the head of submission, the Belgian ambassador, do you know how his name is spelled for the purpose of the record?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: I hope he's not listening, I believe it is d-a [sic] in lowercase, new word, B-a-e-n-s-t, da Baenst.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you very much for that. That's for purposes of the record. Sir, do you have Exhibit 6731 in front of you?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: This is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, if we're going to the trouble of spelling, the -- on line 11, d-a, and Baenst, should it not rather be d-e, because d-a doesn't sound right to me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I agree with you. Actually it would look better e-a, but I -- I -- this is why I hesitate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Okay. We all hesitate, but we have all the options now. Excuse me, Mr. Kruger.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, this is a daily summary from CC Mostar for 18 November 1993. Do you recognise this report?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I wrote this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, if we may look under Political, and there it says HCC. That's you. "Met Slobodan Bozic for lunch. He confirmed Ante Roso as new supreme commander and offered to arrange a meeting." Any comment on that?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: Well, it would -- it announces the departure of General Praljak as the Supreme Commander and we have a male -- we have a name of his successor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Okay. And, sir, if you look at Humanitarian, paragraph 5, the second paragraph first line it seems that the issue of the helicopters is still not solved, and it mentions Medjugorje where the helicopters are.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: Yes. I said earlier I couldn't remember. How I couldn't remember, I don't know, because it should be etched on my mind. It was Medjugorje.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, if we -- sir, the assessment that General Praljak had been -- had gone back, had been -- left his post due to health reasons, as we saw in one of the earlier documents, did you share that assessment or could you comment on that?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: Well, I had no indications as to whether it was healthful or not. It was interesting that the command had changed, and I think when I met Ante Roso, I was very impressed at his military stature, and I could see that we had a serious military commander in place. That is not to be derogatory to General Praljak, but there was a difference in tone. General Praljak had served in the military but not, I believe, as he told me himself, a professional working right up through the ranks to achieve that position, and Ante Roso formed -- informed me at a later meeting of his background, and he had the bearing and sent signals of confidence in his authority as a military commander. I -- but I did not know why Mr. Praljak had -- had gone. I could speculate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, sir, if we can move on to look at Mr. Pusic. You said that you had met Berislav Pusic during the latter part of 1993. Could you give the Court an idea of -- from your dealings with him your view on whether he held or wielded any authority regarding prisoner exchanges and the office that he headed up?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Pusic was one the first leaders of the Bosnian Croats that I -- I met, was introduced to by Jesus Amatriain. He was introduced to me as the person that -- that controlled prisoner of war exchanges, and I believe he was the minister for prisoner of war exchanges. That was certainly my understanding. And all our discussions were around about -- well, movement of people. So it was wider than prisoners of war, because it also included an interest in the movement of Bosnian Croats coming out of Central Bosnia through Serb-held territory. This was something Mr. Pusic was involved with.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: The -- okay. Your ECMM teams, did they monitor these movements of Bosnian Croats out of Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: Only at the points of entry into Herzegovina. In other words, they weren't trailing them or following them through Serb-held territory. And I don't remember us seeing instances, for instance, in Vares which I know was one of the areas that Bosnian Croats came from of them getting onto buses and leaving, and certainly, yes, we tried monitor them when we heard about them arriving in Celebici, as I mentioned to the north earlier, and Stolac was another key point of entry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Was there any particular reason why the moment of these civilians was of interest to the ECMM?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: Well, I think broadly on a number of concerns. Firstly humanitarian. We are talking about some large numbers. We mentioned earlier on the movement of 5.000 people, 5.000 people leaving their homes in Central Bosnia and arriving needing support in their new destination. So there was the humanitarian angle. But also there was -- one could not help but look at the political implications of these moves, particularly when one had been discussing with certain leaders about movements of population. So there was an interest in whether the Croat community was being drawn into a -- a defined territory out of the more vulnerable areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, sir, what about access to detainees in HVO detention facilities? And this is Muslim detainees. Did the ECMM also take an interest in these matters?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: Yes. Could I just add something further to the last question, which I think would -- may be of interest? The other issue about those movements of people was that it indicated that there was a network, a connection, a cooperation between the Bosnian Serbs and the Bosnian Croats, because you could not have that movement without that. So you had that going on, which again was of interest. And to come specifically now to your issue of access to detainees, yes, we raised this with Mr. Pusic. It was consistently an issue for us and for the international community in -- generally.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Did you -- did you raise this with any -- with Jadranko Prlic at any stage that you recall?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: Yes, but I do remember definitively him pointing me toward Mr. Pusic as somebody who should answer this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Okay. May I point you now or direct you now to Exhibit 5976. Exhibit 05976. And this document is from CC Mostar to Zagreb HQ, daily summary for 20 October 1993. Do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: Yes, I recognise it as an ECMM document sent from CC Mostar. It says Daily Summary so it would have been going primarily to regional centre Zenica. However, looking at the date, 20 October, and a number of other small indications that I did not write this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Okay. At the end it says regards Jesus Amatriain and Philip Watkins, HCC and HCC designate Mostar.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: Yes. So that would have been -- yes, as you say, Jesus Amatriain. I'm not sure -- it's likely that he wrote this report. I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Okay. Very briefly the first paragraph, A, political constituents, and it says HCC and HCC designate have met this afternoon Mr. Culjak, and if you look at the comment a few lines down, this was only to introduce yourself, Philip Watkins. Is that basically correct?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, if we turn to the next page under 5, Humanitarian Issues, and we if we look at C, Activities. And there is reference to, "HCC and HCC designate having arranged a meeting with Mr. Pusic on the west side of Mostar. When we arrived, he was not there." And then Dr. Lugonja -- it's reported what he then says. Could you comment on -- on this? Do you have a recollection of this?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: Yeah, it is interesting, and it may bring clarification to something I said earlier. Certainly Mr. Pusic was one of the first Bosnian Croats I saw. I had -- I'd remembered going with Jesus. I think when I finally met Mr. Pusic I was on my own, but on this occasion, yeah, I remember we went there and he was not there but, as it says, here we met his deputy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Do you know anything about that exchange of prisoners that was scheduled for that day?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: No, only in -- in general terms, that there was at a -- at a high level attempts by the ICRC to broker large-scale exchanges of prisoners of war, but there were always local exchanges going on, some of which were sanctioned by ICRC, some of them overseen by ECMM, some of them not involving us at all, just discussions between the warring elements. So I don't specifically know about what this particular exchange was, but the fact that it was happening is -- was not an unusual event.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: While you've raised this issue now, perhaps if you could just briefly give the Court an idea of what was the view from the international perspective regarding the organisation of exchange of prisoners either locally or at a coordinated level internationally?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: Well, the view was that it was a good confidence-building measure. Clearly it was -- something was always raised and are forces being held? Well, if one could try and resolve an exchange of prisoners, then one element of the tensions would -- would hopefully be resolved. It was primarily the responsibility of the ICRC, and they had certain rules and regulations about release of prisoners and where prisoners could go. For instance, I believe that they were -- they found it very difficult to organise exchanges where a prisoner who might come out of captivity but going into an area where they would be vulnerable again was difficult for them, although Bosnia was -- presented that particular organisation with very difficult situation to deal with. It's -- it was, as I say, pockets. So anyone being released and going -- let's say, a Bosnian Muslim being released and going into Bosnian Muslim held territory was still in a vulnerable area. So they had real challenges and difficulties. But they felt certainly as an organisation that it was best dealt with at a senior level.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, if I can refer you to Exhibit 7012. Exhibit 07012. And this is also a daily summary from CC Mostar, dated 2nd of December, 1993. What is interesting on this is even though you're head of CC Mostar, if you look at the last page it is under the name of Roger Castle. Could you comment on this?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: Well, I clearly wasn't there. I don't remember why. It could have been a meeting. I could have been somewhere else, but Roger Castle was a British monitor, part of Mike 1, and was normally based up in Jablanica and covering the area of Jablanica and Konjic. So he finds himself writing the daily report to -- for CC Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Are you able to comment, if we look at page 1, the political situation, and about the middle of that first paragraph it's a reference to Mr. John Bryan. M3 met Mr. John Bryan, and then there's reference to, "the exchange of casualties has started in Mostar and has been successful so far." And then if you go a little bit further down, "Mr. Bryan is hopeful that this exchange will be successful opening the way for the exchange of prisoners and the release of the stranded helicopters." Are you able to comment on this paragraph?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: Yes. It would appear to be an initiative of the ICRC to, if you like, start at that process, but you -- of prisoner exchange, with a view to something larger happening. It's interesting that neither the UN or the ECMM were involved in this, and that's not anything suspicious. As I say, it was the ICRC's clear role and we are just getting information, sharing information amongst the international communities, and on this case Mr. John Bryan is informing us something which the ICRC is doing, and it clearly mentions Mr. Pusic as chief or prison -- of exchange commission. Yeah, that was his official title, not minister, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: The other -- the other names mentioned in -- in this, and if I could ask you if both you and I could also just be a little bit slower for the benefit of the interpreters. If we look at the other names mentioned, apart from Mr. Pusic, it also mentioned Mr. Ivo Sandrk, Tomo Sakota and Mr. Barbaric. Did you know any of these people?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: I don't know Ivo Sandrk. I don't know Tomo Sakota. Mr. Barbaric, his name rings a bell but I don't know any more than that. I do know Mr. Dziho, chief of prisoner of war exchanges from BiH.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, if we could move to the next document in the bundle, which is 07213. 7213.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: Could I note quickly that I also know Mr. Alikadic, just on the name question. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: 7213 is a document dated 16 December, a message from -- or daily summary from CC Mostar to Zagreb headquarters. Do you recognise this report?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I believe this is one of my reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: If we can turn to paragraph 5, humanitarian, on the second page, it's on page 3 in the B/C/S version. And there it says, "Berko Pusic, Croat head of PO war exchange told M9 he had received a fax from ICRC saying that he would not participate in further Muslim prisoner of war releases due to the shooting incident. Nevertheless the Pusic had asked for SpaBat's support to move POWs from Gabela to Jablanica." Do you know -- do you recall this or can you comment on this?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: Well, Mike 9 is me. That's the call-sign number of the head of the centre. Yes, I do remember this. The date is interesting because it is after the an announcement by Mr. Mate Boban of his willingness to unilaterally release prisoners of war, and clearly this has been going on. There's been a specific incident that ICRC have said they will not participate until that particular issue is resolved, but Mr. Pusic is keen to push on and to see more prisoners of war released, and he's looking to UNPROFOR rather than ICRC, and we've offered ECMM presence, I notice, in the comment below. So I think what is happening here is Mr. Pusic is delivering on and looking to continue the -- the prisoner of war exchange and one -- announced by Mate Boban. I think it's an important signal being sent by Mate Boban about cooperation with the international community. And also, of course, if that can be done when the other side are -- are seeing -- being seen not to cooperate that could potentially be good from a PR point of view, but that's not what's being suggested here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
