utterances.text: Just before checking off the document, just two paragraphs down on the same page, there's a reference to Sally Becker and she has a convoy of 70 vehicles, et cetera. This name comes up a few times in some of the documents. Could you perhaps just for the information of the Court very briefly tell us what that was about?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: Sally Becker was known variously as the angel of Mostar. She had essentially arrived in Herzegovina with a convoy and was determined to try and help evacuate casualties from Mostar east. We had failed in an earlier attempt and, as unlikely as it seems, an individual coming in amongst all these international organisations trying to sort something out, various ingredients lined up to actually make this successful, and one of those is she's arriving at a time when the Bosnian Croats are keen to show cooperation. So there wasn't an issue particularly with Sally Becker and Bosnian Croats, and the issue then becomes, will the Bosnian Muslims allow the evacuation? And it was a successful evacuation which we monitored, but at a certain distance. We didn't organise it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you. If we can go to the next document. The very next document in the binder is Exhibit 07226. 7226. And this is once again a daily summary from CC Mostar dated 17 December 1993. Do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: Yes. I wrote this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, if we can look at the general situation at the top, it says, "the release of prisoners of war in accordance with the statement made by Mate Boban is a dominant issue and the report --" and then there's also mention of the Sally Becker issue. Let's have a look at paragraph 5, Humanitarian, on the second page. And here we see that about -- well, first of all there's monitoring of the release of prisoners from Heliodrom near Rodoc, but a few lines down, "Mr. Berko Pusic informed M2 that there will be another release on Monday, 20 December, from the POW camp in Gabela." Could you perhaps just briefly comment on this?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: It's a further indication of the continuing, that time, implementation of Mate Boban's statement, and it also gives us a forward indication of the planning behind this because it's giving us a future date and a number. So there's lots of discussions going on there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Mr. Pusic, was he able to provide statistics beforehand of people who would be released?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: Well, he has on this occasion, yes. And actually, if I remember rightly, on other occasions with regard to movement of populations out of Central Bosnia. We had figures. We were given figures.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, if we go just below that, the POWs released from Heliodrom today were divided into three categories, and then it says so many going to Mostar west, so many going to Mostar east, and then a number going to third countries via Gabela. Could you comment on the destinations of these people?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: Yeah. This was -- where the prisoners went was of interest to the ICRC for the reasons I stated earlier. It was also of interest to both the Bosnian Croats and the Bosnian Muslims. If I deal with the Bosnian -- Bosnian Muslims, they were not happy that the released prisoners went to a third country. They -- it sent the wrong signals, and that was difficult, I think, for the Croats. The Croats were in a strong position wherever the prisoners of war went with one exception. First of all, if they went overseas, well, it sent a signal, didn't it, that these individuals didn't see their future in the Muslim-held territory. If they sent them into -- back into the territory, particularly Mostar east, providing they weren't men of military age, then it actually added to the humanitarian issues that were there, but it signalled a willingness to overcome this big problem of prisoners. We're releasing them and actually if some of them go into that area where they're going to be an extra burden on the humanitarian supplies, well, so be it so we see here there was no consistent movement in POWs but some went overseas. Some went back to Muslim-held territory it. What I don't see here is any indication of those that went into the Muslim-held territory, whether they were of military age, because that would have been a concern because obviously they would have been then eligible to pick up arms and fight against the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, on that, the term POW is used in this report relating to people being released from Heliodrom. Is -- was that in actual fact used in these reports, POW, in its full legal connotation?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: What it meant was simply those detained in -- those that were being held against their will. Prisoners that have -- that had been taken as a result of the fighting between the factions. It may not actually stand the interrogation of a legal definition, but then Bosnia threw up several challenges for legal definitions and I think we get the term displaced persons emerging out of the conflict because we were originally calling them refugees, but unless you cross an international border one is not a refugee. So if they were moving within Bosnia from wherever and concentrating, they were displaced but they weren't refugees. So all we mean by this is prisoners. They may be military, they may be civilians, but people detained against their will by an opposing faction, and it doesn't matter whether it was armija, Serb, or Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Let's look at the first page of this document under Political, the very first paragraph thereof, and this is you talking to Mr. Vladislav Pogarcic, and he says -- he's described as secretary to Mate Boban and member of the presidential council. Then, he confirmed that this new council was "an advisory body only and had no executive powers, but he did say that one of key functions was to allow the CRHB," which is the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, "to operate in the absence of President Boban." Now, my first question on this. He confirmed that this new council. The council he's referring to, is that the council that he's now a member of, the presidential council?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. And it's -- it relates to that earlier document we looked at where I had -- about the Presidency with supporting offices forming, individuals forming around Mate Boban.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, could you comment on the rest of this -- on this paragraph or this piece of the report?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: Well, I said it has no executive powers. We saw it as an advisory body and he seemed to be confirming that, but the -- the statement that its key function was to allow the CRHB to operate in the absence of Boban meant to me one of two things. One, it was simply a secretariat that when Mr. Boban was negotiating in Geneva or Washington or wherever, he had a solid, authoritative body of advice which he could call upon. The other was that perhaps we were seeing an investment now in governmental structures that survive personalities. So certainly Mate Boban was a major personality and had formed a power base around him. In the move from the Croatian Community to the Croatian republic, it was about more structured, more government structures, and government structures must survive personalities. I don't know which he meant, and I don't seem to have pressed him on this occasion. Or indeed if there was an alternatively explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: If we can look about -- just a little bit further than halfway down the -- that paragraph. It says: Regarding the issue of EC administration of Mostar. He said if it led to peace, injection of finance, et cetera, et cetera, he would support it. Could you perhaps just briefly tell the Court what this issue was of EC administration of Mostar?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: Yeah. We rarely received directions from Zagreb as to our activity, but one of the things we did was to explore with all parties the idea which was obviously emerging at an international level recognising that Mostar was a particularly difficult issue. Perhaps one of the elements of a resolution was that it would be administered by the European Union and so I began at every meeting with everybody to explore reactions to that idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Just after that sentence it says: 'The bridges, however, must be the last item on any rebuilding list. However, the city is not negotiable in any settlement and never would be. The Muslims had Sarajevo and Zenica and many more big towns. The CRBH only have one and that is Mostar." Could you comment on that?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: Mostar was presented to the international community as the capital of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, and that it was, as stated here, seen as the -- the only city which they had a major control and presence over, though obviously not an absolute one, and they saw this as the capital and the concern was that any EU administration might dilute the authority of that being seen as a capital. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Let's have a look at another document in regard to this topic, and that is Exhibit 07356. 7356. This is a daily summary from CC Mostar dated 27 December 1993. Do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: Yes, I wrote this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, if we can turn right to the end of the document, paragraph 7, the assessment. And it says here, "Mostar is the stated capital of the CRHB and its importance to the Croats is well-known. The fact remains -- the fact remains the only significant city held by Bosnian Croats as often expressed. Do you have anything to add to that?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: No, but Drago Maric is the person I referred to earlier as a good source of information for what was going on. And it was widely articulated, and had been for some time, that Mostar was Bosnian Croat and that it was going to be the capital of the self-styled republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: In that same paragraph, the fourth -- well, about five or six lines from the bottom there is reference to, "it would underpin their route to the sea." This is something we see in some other documents as well. Could you briefly comment on this issue of route to the sea for Muslims.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: It was always very difficult on the ground to know what was going on at an international level, but in exploring a three-state solution, it was clearly identified that one land-locked element would be any armija -- sorry, any Muslim republic. So a route to the sea seemed to be of -- of enormous importance to discussions going on above, and we know, for instance, that Lord Owen had commissioned a report on Neum as -- as a port, and could that be a route to the sea. There were other possible routes that were looking at going through Montenegro, and occasionally we were meeting these ideas and -- and passing comment, and this is one example.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Okay. If we can briefly look at paragraph 5, Humanitarian. And it says M9. That would be you once again.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: "Attended the weekly humanitarian meeting and were informed by ICRC and then certain statistics about the release of detainees." Is it correct at this stage that the unilateral release of detainees by the HVO was still ongoing?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: Yes, it was. This is the meeting that was chaired by Martin Raguz.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if we can look at the Political section on the first page of this, and here we have -- this is Drago Maric still reporting, and he -- this is in a meeting with you, HCC.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: About halfway down, Maric provides a list of 69 house of representative members, and then he says, "Dario Kordic is a member but not holding office, as is Ignac Kostroman. Anto Valenta, however, is not a member as previously reported." Do you report on this -- could you recall this?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: Yes, more sort of the indication of confusion as to what the roles of those Central Bosnian leaders was going to be, and this was as late as the 27th of December whereas previously we've said with some clear authority that we believe that Kordic is the vice-president of the Presidency and that Valenta is the vice-president of the government, and Mr. Maric here is giving me indications that that -- that isn't the case. But actually, I do believe that we establish very quickly afterwards that this bit of information is wrong and that they were in those key positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, let's move on to this. This was just before the 29th of December, and you mentioned earlier that you had been invited by Mr. Prlic to attend the session of the parliament at which the government would be approved; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: I was invited to attend the first session. I can't remember whether that was the session at which it was going to be approved or whether there had been any other, but I believe it was the first session, and I certainly was invited by Mr. Prlic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, attending this session, did you have an interpreter with you or were you able to follow the proceedings?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: I had an interpreter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Were you actually -- or where did you sit during the session?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: It was a very generous offer of Mr. Prlic, and I'm not sure when I got there that everybody else thought it was such a good idea. We stood out. We were dressed in white. We were internationals, and this was discussions and home truths day, and I nevertheless sat quietly in amongst the seating, in amongst the members, and watched with interest, indeed fascination at what unfolded.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: The interpreter you had with you, did he interpret the proceedings as you went on or did you -- did he tell you afterwards what had happened?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: I don't remember it was a he. I think it was Mija Grubesic but I could be wrong. Normally in meetings it was directs translation. In fact I've just remembered to speak more slowly for the translators. But yes, they would be whispering elements and telling me what was going on but there were also some quite dramatic moments that didn't necessarily need translation. There were interesting things happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Who was -- who delivered the main speech at this -- or these speeches?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: We had a main speech from Mate Boban, which was demonstrative, powerful speech, and we also had a similarly powerful speech and quite a dramatic entrance of lieutenant General Ante Roso, which was very well received. What was of interest to me, though, was that I actually did hear dissent. I heard a number of people question Mate Boban, and indeed Ante Roso from the floor, which was of interest to me because it wasn't quite as -- as constrained; alternative views were being offered. I do remember a speaker from Tuzla, I forget the name, talking about the Posavina Corridor. I do remember Ivo Lozancic from Zepce speaking about uncertainty of political leadership, and I do remember Mr. Roso being asked about the church's position, and I think we saw previously earlier the church had made a statement. I forget what the statement was but it was something obviously of interest at the time. So also quite a dramatic arrival of Mr. Kostroman who was a political advisor to Dario Kordic, and I remember there being some discussion about how had he got out of Central Bosnia. So it was a -- a very interesting day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: The dissenting voices that you heard that you refer to, could you place them geographically regarding their dissent?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: Yes. Zepce and Tuzla, and I guess it reinforces a reference I made earlier that you had a different perspective if you were in Central Bosnia as to -- as to what the future was and maybe you felt vulnerable.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: If we can have a look at Exhibit 07372. 7372. This is a daily summary from CC Mostar, dated 29 December 1993. Do you recognise this?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: Yes. I wrote this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And is this essentially your report on the session that you had attended?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: Yes, it is. And I see another name there which I didn't mention earlier but that Mile Akmadzic made a very interesting speech about the need to send the right signals to the international community. He was indeed in a position of international relations, and I remember him having some authority. There was some gravitas about his presentation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, looking at that first session Political about eight or mine lines down, it says, Boban stated that, "if Muslims and Serbs did not accept the union of republics, then Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna would join Croatia." Could you comment on this?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: Yes. At the 29th of December, there was no groundswell discussion or indeed, in my mind, any likely suggestion of what was actually to follow which was a federation of Croats and Muslims. At the time we all understood that the main option on discussion was a three-republic solution with the attached issues we've touched on. Now, there was posturing as to how that would be achieved, and I think we can then link back to some of the arrival of HV forces and how that was sending signals at the international level, that if those failed there would be an alternative solution, and the alternative solution was a -- a formal link with -- with Croatia, and of course this was invoking concepts about a Greater Croatia. What a ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: When you heard that, was that something new to your ears?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: No, it wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Where had you heard it before or in what context?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: Well, there was a lot of belief and understanding that the motives of the Bosnian Serbs was to create a Greater Serbia, and that of the Croats was a Greater Croatia. I think that the Bosnian Croat position was probably more subtle than that, that, yes, there was to be a union with Croatia, but if that could be achieved through the establishment of -- or if the international community was insisting that Bosnia-Herzegovina remained an integral state but allowed a republic to be set up which was run by the Bosnian Croats, then that would allow -- that would satisfy because ostensibly there was no border between Bosnian Croat activity and Croatia. Yes, there was an international border there but in terms of economic activity and movement, it was seamless.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: If I can refer you to the next page of your report very briefly. Under Humanitarian, of course, you report once again further on release of detainees. But just after that, 6, Other Matters, "with the arrest of the HVO tank crew for the decision of the Old Bridge, Safet Dziho said it was a show trial." Could you comment on that?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: Yes. In November we'd had indicated to us by Mr. Budakovic who was then commanding 4th Corps that the HVO forces were targeting Stari Most bridge. It was subsequently destroyed, and I engaged various members of both military and political about the destruction of this bridge and the explanation given to me was that it had been caused by a renegade HVO tank crew. The tank crew had been arrested and that they were put on trial. And I do remember that one of my monitors Henri Villardsen from Denmark had a legal background, and when that explanation that they were going to go on trial was made, I made it his task to try and watch the development of that -- of that trial. And here Safet Dziho is the commander of the East Mostar brigade. So under Budakovic and, prior to that, under Arif Pasalic, and also you'll note that he was named as somebody who dealt with prisoner of war exchanges earlier. So we're -- we're mentioning this tank crew arrest and Dziho is saying it's just a show trial. It's -- someone's being sacrificed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Were you able to monitor the trial as you had intended or ordered?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: I didn't monitor it, and -- no, I don't even believe that Henri Villardsen saw any more. We did see a report in the press, though; I do remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Can you recall the nature of that report?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: Just a statement that a trial was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Let's move on to the very next document which is Exhibit 07405. 7405. And this is an ECMM daily summary from CC Mostar, dated the 30th of December, 1993. Do you recognise this report?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: Although not signed by me I believe this is my report. I wrote this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Okay. Looking at the very first paragraph, Political, it says, "HCC met Mr. Ivo Tokic and the status of Croatian republic of HB President Mate Boban was discussed." And then it says, "Tokic believed the EU was contributing to rumours of President Boban's replacement after presenting the 14-point document." First of all, do you know what this 14-point document is or was?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: I don't think I ever saw this because I do remember that we -- we asked for information about this, but it -- it was always rather galling when people on the ground told us about EU documents, but we understand that this is being -- this was an EU-generated document, probably in collaboration with UN, that he was referring to; I haven't seen it. And one of those was a requirement that Mate Boban was replaced as part of the solution and finding a way forward.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And could you comment on the notion of the EU approaching Franjo Tudjman with regard to the replacement of Mate Boban or his removal?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: Well, I don't think anyone at an international level saw the solution of Bosnia-Herzegovina as something which would be found by mere reference to the leadership within Bosnia-Herzegovina. It needed both senior leadership of the Serbs and of the Croats to instigate a police -- police -- instigate a peace. So here we see the international community believing that Dr. Franjo Tudjman is a conduit to the Bosnian Croats and that he has the authority to quietly remove Mate Boban. And this builds on what was a continual interest, which I've referred to earlier, as to what was Mate Boban's future, and it had been raised by one of the delegates of the meeting on the 29th of December at that Presidency, where he had said that uncertainty of the leadership was -- was causing issues. So we were interested, where was Mate Boban's future? Was he on the ascendancy? Was he on the way out? And likewise, what was -- who was replacing? Where was the power being held?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Just about -- well, a few lines down. "Tokic informed that some discussion had taken place on key office appointments," then once again we find the issue of central Bosnian politicians being raised. Do you wish to add anything to that?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: I don't think so. I think we've explored it earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Your comment, basically, is contained there as well?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Just very briefly perhaps in the next paragraph we again see that M3 has met Pero Markovic, who is now referred to as president of the Executive Committee, former mayor of Capljina, "have explained about the structure of the party." Could you comment on that?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: Yes. I do remember that one of the elements that came out of the discussion of the formation of the CRHB was the role of political parties and I seem to remember that HDZ was pronounced the only political party and that others like, gosh, HOS, there were a number of fragmented or smaller, should I say, Bosnian Croat parties, but HDZ, if anyone was in any doubt, was going to be the party and Pero Markovic was the leader of the HDZ.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, sir, in the few minutes remaining before our break, perhaps just a few very general issues. To your mind in Herceg-Bosna or Herzegovina, for the Bosnian Croats from your experience in your time there, who provided the political and ideological leadership?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: The ideological leadership, in my opinion, came primarily from Mate Boban and, in Central Bosnia, from Dario Kordic. Their other key elements and key leaders were Jadranko Prlic, clearly Pero Markovic, and some of the others we've mentioned. The difference that -- I would state with Mr. Prlic is I didn't see him as a ideologue. I saw him as an astute survivor politician, more calculating a future, but he wasn't, if you like, the voice of extremism. So a pragmatic politician but a key -- key politician for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Okay. The leadership for the Bosnian community of Herceg-Bosna and -- sorry, what am I talking about, the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna and later the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, where was the -- the key location for that leadership?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS
utterances.text: In Grude and in Mostar, but in Herzegovina. The -- the military leadership was in Citluk and then later Posusje.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Okay. Your Honour, I think this may be a time to break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Registrar, tomorrow you will tell us how long the Prosecution has used. Witness, a few words about tomorrow. You will come back tomorrow at 9.00 a.m. Between now and tomorrow you will meet absolutely no one, because you're under oath. Therefore, you are the witness of the Trial Chamber and not the witness of any other parties. We will resume tomorrow at 9.00 a.m.
